0.title: In the Beginning Was the Word
0.overview:
The Gospel of John is the most theological document ever written. Where Matthew presents Jesus as the King of Israel, Mark as the Servant-Son, and Luke as the Saviour of the world, John presents Jesus as the eternal Word of God who became flesh and dwelt among us — the visible form of the invisible God. John wrote last, having lived longest with the mystery of the incarnation, and every sentence carries the weight of that lifelong meditation.

John's purpose is stated with unusual precision at the end of the book: "these are written so that you may believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God, and that by believing you may have life in his name" (20:31). Two things — belief and life. Not mere assent to facts, but faith in a person; and not mere existence, but the eternal life that is knowing God and knowing Jesus Christ whom he has sent (17:3). The entire Gospel is an extended argument for this faith, structured around seven signs and seven "I AM" declarations.

The seven signs escalate in power and publicity: water to wine (private), healing the official's son (at a distance), healing the invalid (Sabbath controversy), feeding five thousand (crowd), walking on water (disciples alone), healing the blind man (Jerusalem), raising Lazarus (public, four days dead). Each sign is a window into who Jesus is; together they build the case that "no one can do these signs that you do unless God is with him" (3:2) — and more than that: unless he is God. The eighth and final sign is the resurrection itself, which the prologue has been anticipating from its first verse.

The seven "I AM" statements are the theological spine of the Gospel. Each one appropriates the divine name revealed at the burning bush (Exod 3:14 — "I AM WHO I AM") and fills it with the content of Jesus' saving work: I am the bread of life; the light of the world; the door; the good shepherd; the resurrection and the life; the way, the truth, and the life; the true vine. These are not metaphors about a human teacher but divine self-disclosures of the Son of God. When Jesus says "Before Abraham was, I am" (8:58), his hearers pick up stones to throw at him — they know exactly what he is claiming.

Unique to John is the Farewell Discourse (chapters 14–17) — five chapters of intimate instruction given to the disciples on the night of his betrayal. Here Jesus gives his most extended teaching on the Holy Spirit ("another Helper"), on union with him ("abide in me"), on the world's hatred, on the coming joy, and on the prayer that will sustain the church to the end of the age. The High Priestly Prayer of chapter 17 — Jesus praying for his disciples and for all who will believe through their word — is the most sacred text in Scripture. John's Gospel ends not with a commission but with a question: "Do you love me?" Everything hangs on the answer.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–18 — The Prologue: The Word Became Flesh
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: John's Gospel opens not with a manger or a genealogy but with eternity. 'In the beginning was the Word' — the echo of Genesis 1:1 is deliberate and staggering: the one who spoke creation into existence is himself uncreated, personally distinct from God yet fully God. The Prologue is the theological key to the entire Gospel: every miracle, every discourse, every confrontation is the story of the eternal Word living among his own creation. He came to his own, and his own did not receive him — but to all who did receive him, he gave the right to become children of God. The incarnation is both the most glorious and the most rejected event in human history.
verseByVerse.theology: The Word (Logos) is not an abstract philosophical principle but the personal Son of God through whom all things were made and in whom life and light reside. John's Christology is the highest in the New Testament: Jesus is fully God, co-eternal with the Father, the agent of creation, the source of life. The incarnation does not diminish his deity — 'the Word became flesh' while remaining the Word. Grace and truth come through Jesus Christ; the law came through Moses. The contrast is not abolition but fulfillment: the law pointed to the one in whom grace and truth are personally embodied.
verseByVerse.examples: Calvin writes that the Prologue is the key that opens the entire Gospel: whoever grasps who Jesus is before reading a single miracle will interpret everything correctly. Sproul observes that 'the Word was God' (not 'a god') is one of the clearest affirmations of Christ's full deity in all of Scripture. Keller notes that the Logos concept would have resonated with both Jewish (the creative Word of God) and Greek (the rational principle of the universe) audiences — John is announcing that the one both traditions were groping toward has arrived in person.

verseByVerse.quote: "In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God. He was in the beginning with God."
verseByVerse.commentary:
'In the beginning was the Word' — not 'came to be' but 'was.' Before the beginning existed, the Word already existed. There was never a moment when the Word was not. 'With God' — the preposition suggests face-to-face personal relationship, distinction of persons within the Godhead. 'The Word was God' — not a god, not divine in a lesser sense, but fully and essentially God. The Trinity is not yet named but is already present: two persons in eternal communion, both fully God.

That phrase 'not a god' is worth more than an assertion, because a reader may well have had it disputed on his own doorstep. The Jehovah's Witnesses' New World Translation renders the last clause 'the Word was a god,' and the argument offered is that the Greek here has no definite article before 'God' in that final phrase, though it does in the phrase before it. The observation about the article is perfectly correct. The conclusion drawn from it is not.

In Greek, a noun standing before the verb in this construction regularly drops the article and tells you what something is by nature — not which individual it is. John is doing something very precise, and English cannot quite carry it. He needs to say two things at once and not let either swallow the other: the Word is not the same person as the Father (so, 'the Word was with God'), and the Word is nonetheless everything the Father is (so, 'the Word was God'). Had he added the article to that last clause he would have collapsed the two persons into one and denied the distinction he had just made. Had he meant 'a god' he would have written a sentence no Jew could utter, since a second and lesser deity is precisely what Israel's whole faith existed to deny.

And the very next verse closes the door. All things were made through him, and without him was not any thing made that was made. Whatever exists that is not God was made through the Word — so the Word cannot be among the things that were made. There is no room left for a created, junior deity. He stands on the Creator's side of the line, which is the only line the Bible ultimately draws.

verseByVerse.quote: "All things were made through him, and without him was not any thing made that was made. In him was life, and the life was the light of men."
verseByVerse.commentary: The comprehensive scope of creation: 'all things' — nothing that exists came into being apart from the Word. This eliminates any eternal matter independent of God; the Word is not one creative force among many but the sole agent through whom the Father creates. 'In him was life' — not derived life but original, self-existent life. This is the life of God himself, not merely biological existence. This life is the light of men — the source of all rational, moral, and spiritual illumination that humanity possesses.

verseByVerse.quote: "The light shines in the darkness, and the darkness has not overcome it. There was a man sent from God, whose name was John."
verseByVerse.commentary: 'The darkness has not overcome it' — the Greek word can mean both 'overcome' and 'comprehend.' Both meanings apply: the darkness of fallen humanity has neither extinguished the light nor understood it. But the light shines on, undefeated and uncontained. John the Baptist enters the narrative as a man sent from God — not the light itself but a witness to it. The distinction is crucial: even the greatest human prophet is only a witness, not the source.

verseByVerse.quote: "He came as a witness, to bear witness about the light, that all might believe through him. He was not the light, but came to bear witness about the light."
verseByVerse.commentary: John's entire ministry is defined by what he is not: not the light, not the Christ, not Elijah (he will deny this in v. 21), not the Prophet. He is the witness. The function of witness is to point away from oneself toward the one testified to. The purpose of his witness — 'that all might believe through him' — establishes from the outset that faith is the response the Gospel calls for. All the signs, discourses, and encounters in John's Gospel are designed to produce belief.

verseByVerse.quote: "The true light, which gives light to everyone, was coming into the world. He was in the world, and the world was made through him, yet the world did not know him."
verseByVerse.commentary: 'The true light' — genuine and original, as opposed to derivative or shadowy. Every human experience of light, beauty, reason, and goodness is a dim reflection of the one who is the source. 'Gives light to everyone' — the general illumination of common grace through which all humans have some knowledge of God and morality. 'The world did not know him' — the great tragic irony: the Creator enters his own creation and is unrecognized by it. Not ignorance but willful non-recognition.

verseByVerse.quote: "He came to his own, and his own people did not receive him. But to all who did receive him, who believed in his name, he gave the right to become children of God,"
verseByVerse.commentary: 'His own' — Israel, the covenant people prepared through centuries of scripture, prophecy, and promise to receive their Messiah. They did not receive him. But 'all who did receive him' — not a subset of Israel but anyone, Jew or Gentile — receive the right to become children of God. This is adoption: by nature we are not God's children; by grace through faith in Christ we are made so. The receiving and the believing are the same act described from two angles.

verseByVerse.quote: "who were born, not of blood nor of the will of the flesh nor of the will of man, but of God. And the Word became flesh and dwelt among us, and we have seen his glory, glory as of the only Son from the Father, full of grace and truth."
verseByVerse.commentary: The new birth is entirely God's work — not inherited (blood), not chosen by human desire (flesh), not produced by human decision (will of man), but of God. Then the most staggering sentence in the Bible: the Word became flesh. The eternal, uncreated, all-powerful Son of God took on human nature — not pretending, not appearing, but genuinely becoming what he was not while remaining what he was. 'Dwelt among us' — the Greek word is 'tabernacled,' evoking the wilderness tabernacle where God's glory dwelt. He is the new tabernacle, the new meeting place of God and humanity.

verseByVerse.quote: "(John bore witness about him, and cried out, 'This was he of whom I said, "He who comes after me ranks before me, because he was before me."') For from his fullness we have all received, grace upon grace."
verseByVerse.commentary: John the Baptist's testimony inserts itself into the Prologue: the one who comes after me in time existed before me in eternity. The ranking is ontological, not merely chronological. 'From his fullness we have all received, grace upon grace' — the image is of the sea overflowing to fill every vessel that approaches it. The Greek suggests wave upon wave of grace, grace replacing grace, an inexhaustible supply flowing from the one who is himself full of grace and truth.

verseByVerse.quote: "For the law was given through Moses; grace and truth came through Jesus Christ. No one has ever seen God; the only God, who is at the Father's side, he has made him known."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The contrast with Moses is not abolition but fulfillment and surpassing. The law was given — it came from outside, as commandment. Grace and truth came — they arrived in person, embodied. 'No one has ever seen God' — not even Moses, who saw God's back (Exod. 33:23). But the only God who is at the Father's side — reclining at table in intimate fellowship, as John will often picture it — he has made him known. Jesus is the living exegesis of the Father: everything God is, the Son makes visible in human flesh.

Two things in this verse will stop a reader comparing Bibles. The first is that where this version has 'the only God,' an older one has 'the only begotten Son.' That is a genuine difference in the manuscripts, and it is not a small one, since the first reading calls Jesus God outright. The earliest copies we have support 'the only God'; the majority of later ones read 'Son.' Either way the sentence teaches the same thing — the reading with 'Son' still says he is at the Father's side and has made him known, and the whole prologue has already said he is God in verse 1 — but it is worth knowing why your Bible differs from your grandmother's here, and worth noticing that the older manuscript evidence points, if anything, to the higher reading.

The second is the word 'begotten' itself, which has confused generations of readers into thinking it means Jesus had a beginning. It does not. The Greek word means one of a kind, the only one of its sort — Isaac is called by the same word in Hebrews 11:17, though Abraham had another son. It speaks of uniqueness of relationship, not of origin in time. This is exactly why the Nicene Creed insists on the strange-sounding phrase 'begotten, not made': whatever the Son's eternal relation to the Father is, it is not the relation of a creature to its Creator. He was not produced. He is, and always was, the Father's own.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 19–51 — The Testimony of John and the First Disciples
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: John the Baptist's testimony before the Jerusalem delegation is a masterclass in self-emptying: he denies being the Christ, Elijah, or the Prophet, and identifies himself only as 'the voice of one crying in the wilderness.' His entire identity is absorbed by the task of pointing to the one coming after him. The next day he sees Jesus and delivers his greatest sermon in a single sentence: 'Behold, the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world.' Two of his disciples follow Jesus; Andrew finds Simon; Philip finds Nathanael. Each encounter is unique, each testimony is personal, and Jesus's response to Nathanael — 'you will see heaven opened, and the angels of God ascending and descending on the Son of Man' — identifies him as the new Bethel, the true meeting place between heaven and earth.
verseByVerse.theology: The gathering of the first disciples in John 1 is a theology of testimony: John testifies to Jesus; Andrew testifies to Simon; Philip testifies to Nathanael. The gospel spreads through personal witness. Each person who encounters Jesus becomes a testimony to others. The titles accumulate — Lamb of God, Son of God, Rabbi, Messiah, King of Israel, Son of Man — each one true, each one partial, each one pointing toward the one who exceeds all titles. Faith begins with testimony, but it must end with personal encounter: 'Come and see.'
verseByVerse.examples: Keller notes that 'Behold, the Lamb of God' is the most comprehensive atonement statement in the New Testament: the lamb of Passover (Exod. 12), the lamb of the daily sacrifice (Lev. 1), the suffering servant who is led like a lamb to slaughter (Isa. 53:7), and the apocalyptic Lamb who alone is worthy (Rev. 5) — all in one person. Stott observes that Andrew's first act after meeting Jesus is to find his brother: the natural overflow of genuine encounter with Christ is the desire for others to share it.

verseByVerse.quote: And this is the testimony of John, when the Jews sent priests and Levites from Jerusalem to ask him, "Who are you?" He confessed, and did not deny, but confessed, "I am not the Christ."
verseByVerse.commentary: The delegation from Jerusalem is official: priests and Levites represent institutional Judaism come to audit the Baptizer's authority. John's answer is a double confession — he did not deny but confessed — that stresses the voluntary, uncoerced nature of his self-identification. He is not the Christ. The negative precedes the positive in John's testimony, just as the law prepares the way for grace. Reformed theology has always insisted that the herald's glory is entirely derivative: John shines only by reflected light from the one who is the Light itself.

verseByVerse.quote: And they asked him, "What then? Are you Elijah?" He said, "I am not." "Are you the Prophet?" And he answered, "No."
verseByVerse.commentary: The questioners work through Malachi's Elijah and the Mosaic Prophet of Deuteronomy 18 — the two expected forerunners of the messianic age. John denies both titles. He is not a figure in his own right but a voice. Yet Jesus will later say John is Elijah who was to come (Matt. 11:14) — in function, not in person. John's denial is not contradiction but humility: he will not allow the crowds to construct a messianic identity around him that would compete with the one coming after.

verseByVerse.quote: So they said to him, "Who are you? We need to give an answer to those who sent us. What do you say about yourself?" He said, "I am the voice of one crying out in the wilderness, 'Make straight the way of the Lord,' as the prophet Isaiah said."
verseByVerse.commentary: Pressed for a positive identification, John reaches for Isaiah 40:3 — the great comfort passage of the exile's end. He is a voice, nothing more. Not even a messenger with a name, just a sound that announces the coming of one greater. Calvin observes that John's self-effacement is the model for every minister of the gospel: the preacher is the voice; Christ is the Word. Every sermon that exalts the preacher rather than the Lord has confused the voice for the speaker.

verseByVerse.quote: (Now they had been sent from the Pharisees.)
verseByVerse.commentary: This parenthetical note is theologically significant: the delegation is Pharisaic. The Pharisees are the guardians of legal observance, and their concern about John's baptizing without recognized authority will surface again throughout the gospel. Institutional religion is interrogating the prophet. The pattern recurs throughout John: Jerusalem, with its temple and its lawyers, cannot recognize the one it has been waiting for because it has domesticated the waiting into a system.

verseByVerse.quote: They asked him, "Then why are you baptizing, if you are neither the Christ, nor Elijah, nor the Prophet?" John answered them, "I baptize with water, but among you stands one you do not know."
verseByVerse.commentary: The question is jurisdictional: by what authority does an unauthorized nobody wash people in the Jordan? John's answer reframes the entire exchange. The real question is not about John's credentials but about the one standing unrecognized in their midst. The great tragedy of official religion is that it can be so focused on procedural legitimacy that it misses the presence of the Living God. The one they are interrogating John about is already among them — and they do not know him.

verseByVerse.quote: "even he who comes after me, the strap of whose sandal I am not worthy to untie." These things took place in Bethany across the Jordan, where John was baptizing.
verseByVerse.commentary: John borrows the language of a slave's duty — untying the master's sandal — and declares himself unworthy even of that service. The Baptist's self-abasement before Christ is total and deliberate. Bethany across the Jordan places this testimony in concrete geography: the wilderness threshold, the Jordan crossing, the liminal space where Israel once entered the land. Now a new and greater crossing is being announced. The geography of redemption is always particular.

verseByVerse.quote: The next day he saw Jesus coming toward him, and said, "Behold, the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world! This is he of whom I said, 'After me comes a man who ranks before me, because he was before me.'"
verseByVerse.commentary: "Behold the Lamb of God" is the interpretive lens for the entire fourth gospel. The Passover lamb, the suffering servant of Isaiah 53, the daily temple sacrifice — all converge in this cry. Jesus does not merely model redemption or teach about it; he takes away sin, actively bearing and removing it. The ranking paradox — after me yet before me — announces the eternal pre-existence of the one who entered history later than John. Incarnation does not diminish deity; it expresses it.

verseByVerse.quote: "I myself did not know him, but for this purpose I came baptizing with water, that he might be revealed to Israel."
verseByVerse.commentary: John's honest confession — he did not know Jesus by supernatural insight but required the Father's appointed sign — establishes the gospel's epistemological principle: God reveals himself on his own terms and by his own appointed means. John's ministry of water baptism was not self-initiated; it was divinely commissioned for the specific purpose of creating the occasion for revelation. Every ministry is instrumental. The goal is always the unveiling of Christ, not the establishing of the minister.

verseByVerse.quote: And John bore witness: "I saw the Spirit descend from heaven like a dove, and it remained on him. I myself did not know him, but he who sent me to baptize with water said to me, 'He on whom you see the Spirit descend and remain, this is he who baptizes with the Holy Spirit.'"
verseByVerse.commentary: The Spirit's remaining on Jesus distinguishes him from every other anointed figure in Israel's history: prophets, priests, and kings received the Spirit for a season and a task; Jesus bears the Spirit permanently and without measure (3:34). The dove — evoking the Spirit hovering over creation (Gen. 1:2) and the dove that returned with the olive branch (Gen. 8:12) — signals new creation and covenant peace. The one who baptizes with the Holy Spirit can do so because the Spirit rests upon him without diminishment.

verseByVerse.quote: "And I have seen and have borne witness that this is the Son of God."
verseByVerse.commentary: John's final testimony in this section is the gospel's central confession: the Son of God. Some manuscripts read "the Chosen One of God," which is also a rich messianic title. Either way, John's function is complete — he has seen, he has borne witness, and now he recedes. The eyewitness language (I have seen, I have borne witness) is juridical: John is a legal witness whose testimony carries weight because it is grounded in direct perception. The fourth gospel is deeply concerned with the reliability of testimony about Jesus.

verseByVerse.quote: The next day again John was standing with two of his disciples, and he looked at Jesus as he walked by and said, "Behold, the Lamb of God!"
verseByVerse.commentary: On the third consecutive day in this chapter, John repeats his testimony — now to his own disciples. The repetition is deliberate: faithful witness is not one announcement but a sustained, consistent pointing. John looks at Jesus walking by and simply says what he has already said. There is something deeply Reformed in this: the preacher's task is not novelty but fidelity, not new revelation but faithful repetition of the one gospel. Look — there he is. The Lamb of God.

verseByVerse.quote: The two disciples heard him say this, and they followed Jesus.
verseByVerse.commentary: The power of faithful testimony: two disciples hear John and immediately follow Jesus. John loses his followers by pointing them to Christ, and this is his joy and his purpose. Effective ministry always produces this result — the congregation moves from the preacher toward the Savior. Keller notes that the best preaching makes people fall in love with Jesus, not with the preacher. John's disciples do not ask permission; they simply turn and go. The word of witness, when the Spirit attends it, produces immediate response.

verseByVerse.quote: "Jesus turned and saw them following and said to them, 'What are you seeking?' They said to him, 'Rabbi' (which means Teacher), 'where are you staying?' He said to them, 'Come and see.' They came and saw where he was staying, and they stayed with him that day, for it was about the tenth hour."
verseByVerse.commentary: 'What are you seeking?' — Jesus's first words in John's Gospel are a diagnostic question that cuts to the heart of every human life. What is the deep desire behind the following? The disciples' response — 'where are you staying?' — is indirect but honest: they want to be where he is. 'Come and see' — the most important invitation in the Gospel. Not 'here is an argument' but 'come and experience.' The tenth hour (4pm) — they stayed the rest of the day. One afternoon with Jesus changes everything.

verseByVerse.quote: One of the two who heard John speak and followed Jesus was Andrew, Simon Peter's brother. He first found his own brother Simon and said to him, "We have found the Messiah" (which means Christ).
verseByVerse.commentary: The first act of discipleship in John's gospel is evangelism: Andrew finds his brother. We have found — the plural is striking, as if discovery demands sharing. The Messiah: Andrew translates the Hebrew title for John's Greek readers, and in doing so announces the fulfillment of Israel's entire waiting. One afternoon with Jesus, and Andrew knows. This is the nature of encounter with Christ — it is self-authenticating, it produces certainty, and it immediately generates the desire to bring others. The chain of witness has begun.

verseByVerse.quote: He brought him to Jesus. Jesus looked at him and said, "You are Simon the son of John. You shall be called Cephas" (which means Peter).
verseByVerse.commentary: Jesus' first act toward Simon is to rename him. He does not ask Simon's credentials or confirm his readiness; he looks at him with penetrating knowledge — "you are Simon the son of John" — and then announces what Simon will become. Cephas/Peter means rock. The name is prophetic, not descriptive: Simon at this moment is anything but rock-like. But Jesus names people according to what he intends to make them, not according to what they currently are. Election precedes transformation; the new name precedes the new nature.

verseByVerse.quote: The next day Jesus decided to go to Galilee. He found Philip and said to him, "Follow me." Now Philip was from Bethsaida, the city of Andrew and Peter.
verseByVerse.commentary: "Follow me" — Jesus' call to Philip is direct and unmediated, in contrast to Andrew and Peter who came through witness. The divine initiative is sovereign and varied: sometimes God works through testimony, sometimes through direct address. Philip's hometown — Bethsaida, the same village as Andrew and Peter — reminds readers that the first disciples are ordinary Galileans, not Jerusalem elites. The kingdom comes to the margins. The gospel of grace always begins where human pride is least established.

verseByVerse.quote: Philip found Nathanael and said to him, "We have found him of whom Moses in the Law and also the prophets wrote, Jesus of Nazareth, the son of Joseph."
verseByVerse.commentary: Philip echoes Andrew: the first impulse of those who find Jesus is to find others. And Philip frames his testimony in the richest possible terms: Jesus is the one Moses and the prophets wrote about. The entire Old Testament is a forward-pointing testimony to Christ. Philip understands immediately that following Jesus is not abandoning Israel's scriptures but fulfilling them. Every rabbi, prophet, and psalm pointed here. This is the Christian reading of the Hebrew Bible: not replacement but completion.

verseByVerse.quote: Nathanael said to him, "Can anything good come out of Nazareth?" Philip said to him, "Come and see." Jesus saw Nathanael coming toward him and said of him, "Behold, an Israelite indeed, in whom there is no deceit!"
verseByVerse.commentary: Nathanael's skepticism is geographic prejudice — Nazareth was an obscure village without messianic pedigree. Philip's answer is the perfect apologetic: Come and see. Not argument but invitation; not proof but encounter. Jesus' greeting to Nathanael is both discernment and honor: a true Israelite, without deceit, like Jacob made new (Jacob the deceiver becomes Israel the God-wrestler). Jesus sees in Nathanael what Nathanael cannot see in himself — the grace of integrity.

verseByVerse.quote: Nathanael said to him, "How do you know me?" Jesus answered him, "Before Philip called you, when you were under the fig tree, I saw you."
verseByVerse.commentary: Jesus' omniscience breaks through the ordinary: he knew Nathanael before their meeting, saw him in a private moment under the fig tree — a traditional site of Jewish study and prayer. The question "How do you know me?" is Nathanael's proto-confession; he already suspects something extraordinary. Jesus' answer demonstrates divine foreknowledge that is not cold surveillance but intimate attention. He was watching. He knows. This knowing is the foundation of all pastoral comfort: the Good Shepherd knows his sheep by name.

verseByVerse.quote: Nathanael answered him, "Rabbi, you are the Son of God! You are the King of Israel!" Jesus answered him, "Because I said to you, 'I saw you under the fig tree,' do you believe? You will see greater things than these."
verseByVerse.commentary: Nathanael's confession — Son of God, King of Israel — is the fullest so far in the gospel, and it comes from the skeptic. One word of supernatural knowledge produces a comprehensive christological confession. Jesus receives the titles without correction but points forward: you have only begun. The disciples' entire journey will be a movement from initial confession toward deeper understanding. Nathanael believed because of a sign; he will come to believe because of resurrection. Faith grows. It does not remain where it first stands.

verseByVerse.quote: And he said to him, "Truly, truly, I say to you, you will see heaven opened, and the angels of God ascending and descending on the Son of Man."
verseByVerse.commentary: Jesus alludes to Jacob's ladder (Gen. 28:12) — the vision at Bethel where heaven and earth were joined by a stairway of angels. Now Jesus declares himself the ladder. He is the point of contact between the divine and human realms, the one through whom heaven's resources flow to earth and earth's worship ascends to heaven. The Son of Man — Jesus' preferred self-designation — carries both Danielic glory (Dan. 7:13) and the vulnerable humanity of Ezekiel's prophetic address. He is the God-man who is himself the place where God and humanity meet.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–12 — The Wedding at Cana: Water into Wine
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The first sign in John's Gospel is deliberately chosen: Jesus turns water into wine at a wedding in Cana of Galilee. The setting is festive, domestic, and thoroughly human. The need is real but not urgent — running out of wine is an embarrassment, not a tragedy. Yet Jesus's response reveals the character of his kingdom: he provides not just enough but an abundance of the finest wine. The six stone jars used for Jewish purification rites hold the old covenant's cleansing water; they are filled to the brim and transformed. The sign points beyond itself: the old purification is giving way to the new wine of the kingdom, the joy of the messianic age replacing the straining observance of the law.
verseByVerse.theology: John calls the miracles of Jesus 'signs' (semeia) — they are not mere wonders but pointers to a deeper reality. The water-into-wine sign points to who Jesus is (the one who brings the new wine of the kingdom) and what his mission accomplishes (the transformation of the old into the new, abundance replacing scarcity, joy replacing labor). 'His hour had not yet come' — the hour of the cross, the hour of glorification, which will be the ultimate sign to which all others point. The disciples see the sign, believe, and their faith is the intended fruit of every sign in this Gospel.
verseByVerse.examples: Sproul notes that the abundance of the provision — six jars of twenty to thirty gallons each — is a sign of the inexhaustible generosity of the kingdom. Calvin observes that Jesus honors the institution of marriage by performing his first miracle at a wedding. Keller points out that 'the best wine last' is the pattern of the gospel: the world offers its best first and then disappoints, but Christ gives his best at the end — the resurrection, the new creation, the eternal feast.

verseByVerse.quote: On the third day there was a wedding at Cana in Galilee, and the mother of Jesus was there. Jesus also was invited to the wedding with his disciples.
verseByVerse.commentary: The third day resonates throughout John's gospel: it is the day of resurrection, the day when God acts decisively. A wedding in Cana — a marginal village in Galilee — is the setting for the first sign. The incarnate Son of God attends a village wedding as a guest, not as a monarch receiving tribute. This is grace: God present in the ordinary celebrations of ordinary people. Mary is simply "the mother of Jesus" throughout John, never named — she matters as the one who brings Jesus' attention to human need.

verseByVerse.quote: When the wine ran out, the mother of Jesus said to him, "They have no wine."
verseByVerse.commentary: The crisis is social, not mortal — running out of wine at a wedding brought public shame in an honor culture. Mary's report is simply factual: they have no wine. She does not tell Jesus what to do; she tells him what is wrong and trusts him to respond. This is the pattern of intercession: bringing need to Jesus without prescribing the solution. He who is sovereign over all things knows better than the one praying how and when and whether to act. Mary's faith is in his character, not his compliance.

verseByVerse.quote: "And Jesus said to her, 'Woman, what does this have to do with me? My hour has not yet come.' His mother said to the servants, 'Do whatever he tells you.'"
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Woman' — not a term of disrespect in the first century, but a formal address that creates a gentle distance: Jesus is distinguishing his filial relationship from his messianic one. 'My hour has not yet come' — the hour of the cross, when the wine of his blood will be poured out, is the hour toward which everything in John's Gospel moves. Yet Mary's response is the model of faith: she does not argue or explain; she simply tells the servants to obey. She trusts without understanding the timing.

verseByVerse.quote: Now there were six stone water jars there for the Jewish rites of purification, each holding twenty or thirty gallons. Jesus said to the servants, "Fill the jars with water." And they filled them up to the brim.
verseByVerse.commentary: Six jars — one short of the number of completion — holding up to 180 gallons of water for Jewish ritual washing. Jesus does not create new vessels; he transforms existing ones. The water of Jewish purification becomes the wine of messianic joy. Reformation, not abolition: the old order is not destroyed but fulfilled and surpassed. The servants fill them to the brim — lavish obedience that leaves no room for addition. God's grace, when it comes, always exceeds what was expected or requested.

verseByVerse.quote: And he said to them, "Now draw some out and take it to the master of the feast." So they took it.
verseByVerse.commentary: The servants take the water-become-wine to the master of the feast without any explanation. They act in simple obedience to Jesus' word, trusting the result without seeing the transformation. The moment of miracle is private; the servants know what the guests do not. This is the pattern of grace: the work of transformation happens invisibly, through ordinary means (water, stone jars, servants), and the result surpasses all natural expectation. The servants model what every Christian is called to be — obedient carriers of what Christ has made new.

verseByVerse.quote: "When the master of the feast tasted the water now become wine, and did not know where it came from (though the servants who had drawn the water knew), the master of the feast called the bridegroom and said to him, 'Everyone serves the good wine first, and when people have drunk freely, then the poor wine. But you have kept the good wine until now.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The master of the feast, unknowing, pronounces the theological verdict: the best wine comes last. This is the pattern of the kingdom: the world gives its best first and the rest disappoints, but Jesus saves the best for when it is most needed. The servants know the secret; the master does not — knowledge of Christ's power is given to those who obey, not to those who merely observe. 'Kept the good wine until now' — the messianic age, with all its abundance and joy, has arrived.

A question is often asked at this point, and it should be answered rather than sidestepped: was it real wine? It was. The steward's remark settles it — he says that a host serves the good wine first and the poor wine after the guests have drunk freely, which is a comment about what alcohol does to a palate and makes no sense of grape juice. Jesus made something between a hundred and a hundred and fifty gallons of it, and he made it very good, for a village wedding whose family would have been shamed by running dry.

That is worth facing squarely, and it is worth not over-reading. Scripture is entirely capable of holding two things at once: wine is a gift that gladdens the heart of man (Ps. 104:15) and is the standing biblical picture of the joy of the age to come, and drunkenness is a sin the same Scripture condemns without softening (Eph. 5:18), as is putting a stumbling block in a weaker brother's path (Rom. 14:21). Nothing here licenses excess, and nothing here shames the Christian who abstains, whether from conviction or from hard experience. What the sign does say is that the God who came among us was not a killjoy. His first miracle was not a rebuke or a healing but a wedding present, and an extravagant one.

verseByVerse.quote: "This, the first of his signs, Jesus did at Cana in Galilee, and manifested his glory. And his disciples believed in him. After this he went down to Capernaum, with his mother and his brothers and his disciples, and they stayed there for a few days."
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Manifested his glory' — this is John's theological summary of every sign. The miracle is not primarily about wine; it is about the disclosure of who Jesus is. The disciples believe — the intended response to every sign in this Gospel. Belief is not merely intellectual assent; it is personal trust in the one who has revealed himself. The movement to Capernaum, his base of Galilean ministry, follows naturally. The ministry has begun.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 13–25 — The Temple Cleansing and the New Temple
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: John places the temple cleansing at the beginning of Jesus's ministry, where the Synoptics place it at the end. Both are historically accurate — Jesus likely cleansed the temple twice, or John is making a deliberate theological statement by frontloading the event: from the start of his ministry, Jesus is in conflict with the temple establishment and its corrupted worship. 'Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up' — the disciples will understand this only after the resurrection. Jesus himself is the new temple, the true meeting place of God and humanity, the one through whom all access to the Father now comes.
verseByVerse.theology: The temple cleansing is an act of prophetic authority: Jesus acts as the Lord coming suddenly to his temple (Mal. 3:1), purifying the house of prayer from the commercial transactions that have turned worship into a market. The zeal that consumes him is zeal for the Father's house — the passion of the Son for the honor of the Father. 'My Father's house' — his first recorded words in Luke (2:49) and his claim here: the temple belongs to his Father, and he has authority over it because he is the Son.
verseByVerse.examples: Calvin notes that the buying and selling were not wicked in themselves but had invaded the sacred space set apart for prayer, turning the house of God into a place of commerce. The sign of the temple's destruction and raising in three days is the central sign of the entire Gospel: the cross and resurrection are the ultimate manifestation of Jesus's glory, the event to which all other signs point.

verseByVerse.quote: The Passover of the Jews was at hand, and Jesus went up to Jerusalem. In the temple he found those who were selling oxen and sheep and pigeons, and the money-changers sitting there.
verseByVerse.commentary:
John places the temple cleansing early in Jesus' ministry — a deliberate theological statement. The Synoptics place it in Passion Week; John places it at the outset, framing Jesus' entire ministry as confrontation with corrupt religion. The temple courts have become a marketplace: animals for sacrifice sold at premium prices, currency exchanged at exploitative rates. What was designed as a house of prayer for all nations has become an economy of exclusion. Religion divorced from God's character always becomes commerce.

But the placement itself is the most-discussed difficulty in this Gospel, and it deserves more than a passing note, because saying John 'placed' it here can sound to a careful reader like saying John moved it. Matthew, Mark and Luke all put a temple cleansing in the last week of Jesus's life, days before the crucifixion. John puts one at the very beginning, with two and a half years of ministry still to run. So what happened?

There are two serious answers and a Christian may hold either. The first is the simplest: it happened twice. That is not the strained solution it sounds. The abuse was structural and profitable and would have resumed within a month of any one-off protest, and the details in the accounts differ in ways that fit two occasions rather than one — here Jesus makes a whip of cords and speaks of 'my Father's house,' while in the Synoptics he quotes Isaiah and Jeremiah about a house of prayer and a den of robbers. The authorities' question differs too. A man who did this once and was not stopped would be very likely to do it again, and a movement that began and ended with the same act of protest is entirely coherent.

The second answer is that John, who is writing last and openly arranges his material by theme rather than by calendar, has set this episode at the front as the doorway into everything that follows. That is not a claim that he invented anything or shifted a date to deceive; ancient writers were free to order true events for meaning, and John tells us plainly that he is selecting (20:30-31). On this reading the cleansing stands here for the same reason the prologue does — to say at the outset who this is and what he has come to do.

Either way the point of the scene is untouched, and it is worth holding on to when the chronology debate has run its course. The Lord has come to his temple, exactly as Malachi said he would (Mal. 3:1), and the first thing he does there is turn over the furniture.

verseByVerse.quote: And making a whip of cords, he drove them all out of the temple, with the sheep and oxen. And he poured out the coins of the money-changers and overturned their tables. And he told those who sold the pigeons, "Take these things away; do not make my Father's house a house of trade."
verseByVerse.commentary: The whip of cords, the overturned tables, the scattered coins — Jesus' action is deliberate, physical, and prophetic. This is not a moment of uncontrolled anger but of holy zeal acting out judgment. My Father's house: the possessive claim is simultaneously a christological statement (he is the Son) and a prophetic indictment (they have profaned what belongs to God). Calvin notes that Jesus cleanses the temple precisely so that genuine worship can take place. Reformation always begins with the clearing out of what has defiled the holy.

verseByVerse.quote: "His disciples remembered that it was written, 'Zeal for your house will consume me.' So the Jews said to him, 'What sign do you show us for doing these things?'"
verseByVerse.commentary: Psalm 69:9 is applied to Jesus: the zeal of the Son for the Father's honor burns as it burned in the psalmist. The disciples' memory of scripture is the interpretive key to understanding Jesus's action. The Jewish leaders' response is not theological reflection but a demand for credentials: what sign? They want authorization, proof of authority. But the sign Jesus will give them is not one they can evaluate on their terms — it is the sign of the resurrection, which requires faith to receive.

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus answered them, "Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up." The Jews then said, "It has taken forty-six years to build this temple, and will you raise it up in three days?"
verseByVerse.commentary: Jesus' riddling word will follow him to the cross (Matt. 26:61) and become evidence at his trial. The authorities hear an architectural claim and respond with architectural logic: forty-six years of Herodian construction cannot be undone and redone in seventy-two hours. They are not wrong about their temple; they are catastrophically wrong about his. The pattern of misunderstanding in John is not stupidity but spiritual blindness: the natural mind cannot perceive the things of the Spirit without new birth.

verseByVerse.quote: But he was speaking about the temple of his body. When therefore he was raised from the dead, his disciples remembered that he had said this, and they believed the Scripture and the word that Jesus had spoken.
verseByVerse.commentary: John's editorial explanation is the interpretive key: the temple is his body. Jesus is himself the locus of God's presence, the place where heaven and earth meet, the dwelling of the divine glory. When the resurrection came, the disciples' memory connected back to this word and produced faith — not just in the resurrection but in the Scripture that foretold it. Resurrection does not only vindicate Jesus; it illuminates everything he said and everything the Old Testament promised. The resurrection is the hermeneutical event that makes all Scripture legible.

verseByVerse.quote: Now when he was in Jerusalem at the Passover Feast, many believed in his name when they saw the signs that he was doing. But Jesus on his part did not entrust himself to them, because he knew all people.
verseByVerse.commentary: Sign-faith — believing because of miracles — is a real but fragile beginning. Jesus receives these believers but does not entrust himself to them. The Greek word for "entrust" is the same as "believe": they believed in him, but he did not believe in them. This is not cynicism but omniscience: Jesus knows the difference between intellectual assent to evidence and the saving faith that perseveres through suffering and offense. Not all who follow the miracle-worker will follow the crucified one. Keller notes that many want Jesus' blessings without Jesus himself.

verseByVerse.quote: and needed no one to bear witness about man, for he himself knew what was in man.
verseByVerse.commentary: Jesus' knowledge of the human heart is comprehensive and unsolicited — he needs no information about people because he already knows. This divine omniscience is both terrifying and comforting: terrifying because nothing is hidden from him, comforting because his love is not naive. He knows the worst about every person and loves anyway. The one who "knew what was in man" chose to give himself for that very man. The cross is not an act of ignorance; it is an act of full-knowledge love, offered in the face of complete understanding of human sin.

2.title: The First Sign: Water into Wine

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–21 — Nicodemus and the New Birth
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Nicodemus comes by night — a detail that is both literal and symbolic. He is a Pharisee, a ruler of the Jews, a teacher of Israel; he comes with flattery and openness, and Jesus cuts through all of it with the most radical statement in the Gospels: 'Unless one is born again, he cannot see the kingdom of God.' The new birth is not religious improvement or moral reformation; it is a sovereign act of the Spirit, as unpredictable and uncontrollable as the wind. Nicodemus, the teacher of Israel, cannot comprehend it — his very inability illustrates the need for it. The conversation ascends to the highest theological altitude in the Gospel: John 3:16, the summary of the entire Bible.
verseByVerse.theology: The new birth is the work of the Spirit, who blows where he wills. No human being can produce it, control it, or predict it; the Spirit sovereignly regenerates those whom God has given to the Son. The lifting up of the Son of Man — as Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness — is the means by which eternal life comes to those who look in faith. God's motive is love for the world; his means is the gift of his Son; his purpose is salvation, not condemnation. The light has come, and the verdict of each person is revealed by whether they come to the light or flee from it.
verseByVerse.examples: Calvin writes that 'born again' (or 'born from above') is the most comprehensive description of salvation in the New Testament: it captures the totality of the transformation (rebirth, not reform), its source (from above, from God), and its necessity (without it, the kingdom cannot be seen). Sproul notes that Nicodemus's night visit is the first of several encounters in John where the darkness represents the condition of the human soul before the light breaks in. Keller observes that John 3:16 is not a formula to be memorized but a universe to be explored: every word contains inexhaustible depth.

verseByVerse.quote: Now there was a man of the Pharisees named Nicodemus, a ruler of the Jews. This man came to Jesus by night and said to him, "Rabbi, we know that you are a teacher come from God, for no one can do these signs that you do unless God is with him."
verseByVerse.commentary: Nicodemus has every credential the world honors: Pharisee, ruler, teacher of Israel. He comes by night — whether from fear of colleagues or in the darkness of spiritual incomprehension, John's night is never merely chronological. His opening is courteous and theologically generous: he acknowledges Jesus as a God-sent teacher authenticated by signs. But this generous assessment, while more than his colleagues offer, is still catastrophically insufficient. A teacher come from God is not the same as the eternal Son of God. Nicodemus has not yet seen what he needs to see.

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus answered him, "Truly, truly, I say to you, unless one is born again he cannot see the kingdom of God."
verseByVerse.commentary: Jesus does not answer the compliment; he answers the need. Nicodemus has not asked a question, but Jesus hears the one beneath the pleasantries: how do I enter the kingdom? The answer is total: new birth. Not reformation, not education, not religious advancement — birth from above. This is the Reformation's great rediscovery: grace is not the improvement of nature but its replacement, not the assistance of the will but its regeneration. You must be born again is not a demand that Nicodemus comply but a declaration of what God alone can do.

verseByVerse.quote: Nicodemus said to him, "How can a man be born when he is old? Can he enter a second time into his mother's womb and be born?" Jesus answered, "Truly, truly, I say to you, unless one is born of water and the Spirit, he cannot enter the kingdom of God."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Nicodemus's question is not absurd; it is the honest bewilderment of natural reason confronting supernatural necessity. He takes Jesus seriously enough to push back. Born of water and the Spirit — the most debated phrase in this passage — likely evokes Ezekiel 36:25-27 where God promises to sprinkle clean water (purification) and put his Spirit within his people. The new birth is the fulfillment of the new covenant promise: God himself will do what Israel could not do, cleansing and transforming from within.

Since it really is the most debated phrase here, the other readings deserve naming. Some take the water to mean Christian baptism, and read the verse as teaching that baptism is the instrument of the new birth — the historic position of Rome and, in a different form, of Lutheran teaching. Some take it to mean natural birth, the water of the womb, so that Jesus is saying a man must be born once physically and once spiritually. Others take it as John's baptism of repentance: you must come by the road John has been preaching, and then receive the Spirit.

The Ezekiel reading remains the strongest, and the reason is Jesus's own rebuke two verses later. He expects Nicodemus, as the teacher of Israel, to have known this already — which points to something Nicodemus could have read in his Bible, not to a Christian sacrament that did not yet exist. Ezekiel 36 puts the water and the Spirit together in exactly this order, in exactly this promise, and Nicodemus should have recognised it on the spot.

On baptism, the fair thing to say is that this verse cannot be made to carry the weight of baptismal regeneration on its own, and that the wider witness of the Gospel runs the other way: John says repeatedly that it is believing that gives life (1:12; 3:15; 20:31), and the dying criminal at Luke 23:43 receives Paradise unbaptised. Baptism is the sign of this birth and a precious one. It is not the machinery of it. What Jesus presses on Nicodemus is not a rite he has missed but a work of God he cannot perform on himself.

verseByVerse.quote: "That which is born of the flesh is flesh, and that which is born of the Spirit is spirit."
verseByVerse.commentary: The principle is ontological: flesh produces flesh; Spirit produces spirit. Natural birth, however extraordinary the parents, cannot produce spiritual life. This is total depravity stated with compressed precision — not that the flesh is worthless in every sense, but that it is categorically incapable of generating the life of God. The new birth is not the improvement of the old nature but the creation of a new one. Sproul notes that we do not cooperate in our own birth; the initiative, the power, and the completion belong entirely to the Spirit who blows where he wills.

verseByVerse.quote: "Do not marvel that I said to you, 'You must be born again.' The wind blows where it wishes, and you hear its sound, but you do not know where it comes from or where it goes. So it is with everyone who is born of the Spirit."
verseByVerse.commentary: 'You must be born again' — the 'you' in Greek is plural: not just Nicodemus but the Pharisees, the rulers, the whole of religious Israel. The wind analogy is precise: the Spirit's work is real and perceptible (you hear the sound) but not traceable or controllable by human observation (you do not know where it comes from or goes). The new birth is sovereign, mysterious, and undeniable in its effects. No one can predict who will be born again, or when, or trace the exact path of the Spirit's movement in a human soul.

verseByVerse.quote: "How can these things be?" Nicodemus asked. Jesus answered him, "Are you the teacher of Israel and yet you do not understand these things?"
verseByVerse.commentary: Nicodemus's second "How?" is deeper than his first: not mocking incredulity but genuine confusion. Jesus' response is gentle but pointed — the teacher of Israel should recognize the contours of the new covenant promised in Ezekiel and Jeremiah. The failure is not intellectual but spiritual: the Scriptures he has spent his life studying were pointing to exactly this, and he has not seen it. Expert knowledge of the Bible does not guarantee encounter with its subject. Knowing the text and knowing the God of the text are not automatically the same thing.

verseByVerse.quote: "Truly, truly, I say to you, we speak of what we know, and bear witness to what we have seen, but you do not receive our testimony. If I have told you earthly things and you do not believe, how can you believe if I tell you heavenly things?"
verseByVerse.commentary: The "we" is striking — Jesus speaks as the representative of a divine communion, bearing witness to what God knows from within. The testimony is rejected not for lack of evidence but for lack of spiritual receptivity. The argument moves from the less to the greater: if you cannot receive the earthly analogy (wind, birth), how will you receive the heavenly reality it points to? Revelation always exceeds comprehension; faith always outruns sight. Nicodemus is being called to trust a witness whose knowledge of heavenly things surpasses all earthly verification.

verseByVerse.quote: "No one has ascended into heaven except he who descended from heaven, the Son of Man. And as Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, so must the Son of Man be lifted up."
verseByVerse.commentary: Jesus grounds his heavenly authority in his heavenly origin: he can speak of heavenly things because he has come from heaven. No mystic, no prophet, no ascent-tradition figure has this — the Son of Man alone has descended. Then the pivot: the serpent of bronze lifted on a pole in the wilderness (Num. 21:8-9) becomes a type of crucifixion. Those who looked to the lifted serpent lived; those who look to the lifted Son of Man will have eternal life. The cross is not an accident; the must signals divine necessity — it must be so because God's redemptive plan from the beginning required it.

verseByVerse.quote: "that whoever believes in him may have eternal life."
verseByVerse.commentary: The scope of the promise is universal in offer and particular in application: whoever — any who will — believes. Eternal life is not merely life extended in duration but life of a new quality, the very life of God shared with those who trust in the lifted Son of Man. Sproul emphasizes that this eternal life begins now, not at death — the one who believes already possesses what death cannot take. Nicodemus came seeking the kingdom; Jesus offers something more — not merely entry into the kingdom but the life of the King himself.

verseByVerse.quote: "For God so loved the world, that he gave his only Son, that whoever believes in him should not perish but have eternal life. For God did not send his Son into the world to condemn the world, but in order that the world might be saved through him."
verseByVerse.commentary:
'So loved' — the adverb points to the manner and degree of the love: in this way, to this extent. 'The world' — not just Israel but the whole of fallen humanity, the object of God's love despite its rebellion. 'His only Son' — the gift is not an angel, not a prophet, not a lesser being but the Father's own eternal Son. 'Whoever believes' — the scope is universal; the condition is faith. 'Should not perish but have eternal life' — the two destinies are perishing and life; the distinction is not natural but covenantal. The Son is sent to save, not to condemn — the condemnation is already there; the mission is rescue.

One practical note, since a reader may have noticed it and wondered. Is Jesus still speaking here, or has John taken over? Bibles disagree visibly: some close the quotation marks at the end of verse 15, which makes the best-known sentence in the Bible John's own comment rather than a saying of Jesus; others run the speech on to verse 21. In a red-letter edition the verse may be printed in red or in black depending on which publisher you happen to be holding.

The honest answer is that we cannot be certain, because the earliest manuscripts have no quotation marks at all — punctuation is the editor's judgement, not the apostle's. There are reasons for thinking John is now reflecting: the tense shifts to the past, God's giving of his Son is spoken of as a completed thing, and the phrase 'only Son' is one John uses in his own voice elsewhere (1:14, 18; 1 John 4:9). Others reply that nothing in the passage signals a change of speaker and the thought runs on unbroken from the serpent in the wilderness.

What is worth saying plainly is that nothing whatever hangs on it. If John wrote it, it is the Spirit-carried testimony of the apostle who leaned on Jesus's chest, and it is Scripture. If Jesus said it, it is Scripture. The words are not more true in red ink. And either way they are the settled summary of what the man in front of Nicodemus had come to do.

verseByVerse.quote: "Whoever believes in him is not condemned, but whoever does not believe is condemned already, because he has not believed in the name of the only Son of God. And this is the judgment: the light has come into the world, and people loved the darkness rather than the light because their works were evil."
verseByVerse.commentary: 'Condemned already' — the natural state of humanity apart from Christ is not neutral; it is already under judgment. The coming of Jesus does not introduce condemnation; it introduces the possibility of escape from a condemnation that was already in place. 'People loved the darkness' — the judgment is not arbitrary; it reflects the settled preference of the human heart. The darkness is comfortable because it conceals the evil of human works. The light is unwelcome because it reveals them. The verdict of the last day is simply the disclosure of the verdict already present in each person's response to Christ.

verseByVerse.quote: "For everyone who does wicked things hates the light and does not come to the light, lest his works should be exposed. But whoever does what is true comes to the light, so that it may be clearly seen that his works have been carried out in God."
verseByVerse.commentary: The movement toward or away from Christ is morally diagnostic: it reveals the orientation of the heart. Those whose works are evil flee the light instinctively, not because the light is bad but because exposure is unwelcome. Those who 'do what is true' — who are oriented toward reality and God — come to the light, because they want their works to be seen as what they are: carried out in God. This is not a works-righteousness system but a description of the spiritual trajectory of genuine faith versus settled unbelief.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 22–36 — John's Final Testimony: The Bridegroom's Friend
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: John the Baptist's final testimony in this Gospel is the most beautiful articulation of humble submission in the New Testament. When his disciples come to him alarmed that Jesus's ministry is drawing larger crowds, John does not feel threatened. He feels fulfilled. 'He must increase, but I must decrease' — eight words that define the entire posture of the genuine servant of God. John is the friend of the bridegroom, not the bridegroom; his joy is complete when he hears the bridegroom's voice and can step aside. The one who comes from above is above all; what he testifies to is true; whoever receives his testimony has set their seal to this: God is true.
verseByVerse.theology: John the Baptist's final words in this Gospel are also its most concentrated theological summary: Jesus comes from above, speaks the words of God, gives the Spirit without measure, and holds in his hands both eternal life and God's wrath. There is no middle ground: whoever believes in the Son has eternal life; whoever does not obey the Son will not see life, but the wrath of God remains on him. The Baptist who began by pointing to the Lamb of God ends by declaring the eternal stakes of the decision about him.
verseByVerse.examples: Keller notes that 'he must increase, I must decrease' is the defining characteristic of all genuine ministry — the minister who builds his own kingdom rather than Christ's has misunderstood the calling. Stott observes that the image of the friend of the bridegroom captures perfectly the joy of the one who serves another's marriage rather than his own: he is not jealous, not diminished, but fulfilled in the fulfillment of the one he loves.

verseByVerse.quote: After this Jesus and his disciples went into the Judean countryside, and he remained there with them and was baptizing. John also was baptizing at Aenon near Salim, because water was plentiful there, and people were coming and being baptized.
verseByVerse.commentary: The parallel ministries of Jesus (through his disciples, as 4:2 clarifies) and John in the Judean countryside create the occasion for the Baptist's final great testimony. Both are baptizing, both are drawing crowds — yet they are not rivals. John's ministry at Aenon near Salim (the exact location is uncertain but Samarian) continues its appointed function: preparing people through repentance and washing. The geography of grace is generous; the Spirit was moving simultaneously in multiple places through multiple servants.

verseByVerse.quote: (for John had not yet been put in prison)
verseByVerse.commentary: This parenthetical note anchors John's gospel chronologically in relationship to the Synoptics, where John's imprisonment marks the beginning of Jesus' Galilean ministry (Mark 1:14). Here the two ministries overlap — a period the Synoptics pass over quickly but John lingers on, because this overlap produces John's most profound testimony about the relationship between the herald and the bridegroom. The parenthesis is not editorial fussiness; it is a temporal marker that helps readers locate this climactic testimony in redemptive history.

verseByVerse.quote: Now a discussion arose between some of John's disciples and a Jew over purification. And they came to John and said to him, "Rabbi, he who was with you across the Jordan, to whom you bore witness — look, he is baptizing, and all are going to him."
verseByVerse.commentary: The disciples' report is tinged with jealousy on their master's behalf: all are going to him. They expect John to be troubled by the competition. The dispute over purification rituals provides the occasion for the question of authority — whose baptism counts, whose ministry is authentic? The disciples are thinking in terms of religious competition; John is thinking in terms of divine purpose. Competitive ministry — measuring one church against another, one preacher against another — always misunderstands the nature of service to Christ.

verseByVerse.quote: John answered, "A person cannot receive even one thing unless it is given him from heaven."
verseByVerse.commentary: John's first answer cuts to the root of all ministry theology: everything is gift, nothing is earned or accumulated. If Jesus is drawing more followers, it is because heaven has given it. If John's crowds are diminishing, it is because heaven has arranged it. Sovereignty over ministry success belongs entirely to God. This single sentence dismantles every form of ministerial envy, rivalry, or pride. The one who understands that everything comes from heaven has no reason to be threatened by another's abundance, because he knows his own abundance (and shortage) comes from the same source.

verseByVerse.quote: "You yourselves bear me witness, that I said, 'I am not the Christ, but I have been sent before him.' The one who has the bride is the bridegroom. The friend of the bridegroom, who stands and hears him, rejoices greatly at the bridegroom's voice. Therefore this joy of mine is now complete."
verseByVerse.commentary: John reaches for the wedding metaphor to describe his relationship to Jesus. The bridegroom is Christ; the bride is the people of God; John is the best man — the shoshben in Hebrew tradition who arranges the marriage and stands with the groom. The best man's joy is complete when he hears the bridegroom's voice speaking to the bride. This is the purest description of gospel ministry: arranging the encounter between Christ and his people, then stepping back in joy when the meeting happens. Joy that is complete is joy that has achieved its purpose.

verseByVerse.quote: "He must increase, but I must decrease."
verseByVerse.commentary: The most profound ministerial theology in Scripture, in seven words. Must increase, must decrease — both are divine necessities, not human preferences. John does not choose to decrease as a pious gesture; the must signals that this is the appointed order of redemptive history. Jesus' glory is not competitive with John's; it is its completion. As Stott observes, any preacher, teacher, or leader who does not have this as their conscious ambition has confused themselves with the one they serve. The herald's glory is to become unnecessary once the King has arrived.

verseByVerse.quote: "He who comes from above is above all. He who is of the earth belongs to the earth and speaks in an earthly way. He who comes from heaven is above all. He bears witness to what he has seen and heard, yet no one receives his testimony."
verseByVerse.commentary: Whether these are John the Baptist's words or the Evangelist's reflection (the transition is debated), the theology is clear: origin determines authority. He who comes from above speaks with heavenly authority; he who is of the earth — even the greatest prophet — speaks from earthly perspective. Jesus' testimony is heavenly because his origin is heavenly. Yet no one receives his testimony: the most authoritative witness in history is the most rejected. This is the scandal of the incarnation — God speaks and the world stops its ears.

verseByVerse.quote: "Whoever receives his testimony sets his seal to this, that God is true."
verseByVerse.commentary: To believe Jesus is to certify God's truthfulness. Faith is not merely personal benefit; it is a public declaration about God's character. The one who trusts Christ affixes a seal — a legal metaphor — attesting that what God has said is true. Conversely, to reject Christ's testimony is to call God a liar (see 1 John 5:10). Faith and unbelief are not merely personal choices; they are theological positions about the integrity of God. The gospel stakes everything on the truthfulness of the Father who sent the Son.

verseByVerse.quote: "For he whom God has sent utters the words of God, for he gives the Spirit without measure. The Father loves the Son and has given all things into his hand."
verseByVerse.commentary: The one God sent speaks God's words — not in the partial, mediated manner of the prophets who received the Spirit for specific occasions — but without measure. The Spirit's fullness in Christ is qualitatively different from every previous anointing in Israel's history. And the foundation of all this is the Father's love for the Son: the mission of the Son flows from the eternal love of the Trinity. The Father gives all things into the Son's hand because he loves him. Mission is always downstream of the eternal love within the Godhead.

verseByVerse.quote: "Whoever believes in the Son has eternal life; whoever does not obey the Son shall not see life, but the wrath of God remains on him."
verseByVerse.commentary: The chapter that began with new birth ends with the sharpest possible alternative: eternal life or the abiding wrath of God. The symmetry of "believes" and "does not obey" reveals that saving faith is not mere intellectual assent but covenantal allegiance — it includes obedience. The wrath of God is not a future threat but a present condition: it remains on those who reject the Son. Calvin is clear that this wrath is not God's caprice but his settled, holy displeasure against all that contradicts his character. The only escape is the Son — precisely because the Son bore that wrath in his body on the tree.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–42 — The Woman at the Well
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Jesus's conversation with the Samaritan woman is the longest one-on-one dialogue in the Gospels. Every element of the encounter crosses a boundary: Jesus crosses from Judea to Samaria, from Jewish to Samaritan territory; he speaks to a woman alone at a well, violating social convention; he engages with someone of scandalous personal history; he reveals himself as the Messiah to an outsider before he does so publicly to his own people. The conversation moves from physical water to living water, from the woman's five husbands to the question of true worship, from worship in Jerusalem or Gerizim to worship in Spirit and truth. The woman who came alone to the well in the midday heat returns to her village as the first evangelist in John's Gospel.
verseByVerse.theology: The living water Jesus offers is not a religious program or a moral reformation; it is himself — the inexhaustible source of eternal life. 'The water that I will give him will become in him a spring of water welling up to eternal life.' Jesus does not merely point to the source of life; he is the source. The worship in Spirit and truth for which the Father seeks is not worship in a particular location but worship in the reality of who God is (truth) and by the power of God's own Spirit — the worship that the new covenant makes possible through the regeneration that Nicodemus could not understand.
verseByVerse.examples: Keller notes that Jesus's method with the Samaritan woman is a model of contextual evangelism: he begins with her felt need (water), moves to her deeper need (the living water), exposes the root issue (her relationships), and leads her to the question of worship and the identity of the Messiah. He does not condemn; he illumines. Calvin observes that the woman's testimony — 'Come, see a man who told me all that I ever did' — is the most basic form of Christian witness: here is someone who knows me completely and has not rejected me.

verseByVerse.quote: Now when Jesus learned that the Pharisees had heard that Jesus was making and baptizing more disciples than John (although Jesus himself did not baptize, but only his disciples),
verseByVerse.commentary: The Pharisees are tracking the growth of Jesus' ministry with the metric of discipleship numbers — a measure John's gospel immediately qualifies: Jesus himself did not baptize. The clarification matters: the growth is not a personal empire-building project but the movement of the Spirit through servants. When religious authorities begin measuring ministries by numbers, they have already confused the kingdom of God with institutional competition. Jesus does not flee Jerusalem because he fears the Pharisees but because his hour has not yet come — everything is governed by divine timing.

verseByVerse.quote: he left Judea and departed again for Galilee. And he had to pass through Samaria.
verseByVerse.commentary: The geographical had to is not topographical necessity — a Jewish traveler could go around Samaria — but divine compulsion. The Spirit was driving Jesus through territory Jews typically avoided: Samaritans were considered half-breed apostates, the unclean residue of Assyrian deportations mixed with foreign settlers. That Jesus had to go through Samaria is John's announcement that the gospel will not respect the ethnic boundaries that religious tradition has erected. Every human barrier that excludes the seeker from the Savior is, for Jesus, an occasion for crossing.

verseByVerse.quote: So he came to a town of Samaria called Sychar, near the field that Jacob had given to his son Joseph. Jacob's well was there; so Jesus, wearied as he was from his journey, was sitting beside the well. It was about the sixth hour.
verseByVerse.commentary: The geography is thick with covenant memory: Sychar near Shechem, the field of Jacob's inheritance, the well that Jacob dug. Jesus sits at the intersection of Israel's patriarchal past. And he is weary — genuinely, physically tired, the weariness of a man who has been walking in the midday heat. The incarnation is not a divine costume; Jesus' exhaustion is real. The one through whom all things were made (1:3) now rests at the well his ancestor dug, waiting for the Father's appointment with a woman no one expected.

verseByVerse.quote: A woman from Samaria came to draw water. Jesus said to her, "Give me a drink."
verseByVerse.commentary: Everything about this encounter violates convention. The hour is wrong (noon, when respectable women did not come to the well), the gender is wrong (a Jewish man does not address an unknown woman), the ethnicity is wrong (no dealings between Jews and Samaritans). Jesus violates every protocol without apology. The request — Give me a drink — opens the conversation from a position of need; he asks her for help before offering her anything. This is grace approaching the outcast without condescension: he who has everything presents himself as needy in order to create the space for encounter.

verseByVerse.quote: (For his disciples had gone away into the city to buy food.) The Samaritan woman said to him, "How is it that you, a Jew, ask for a drink from me, a woman of Samaria?" (For Jews have no dealings with Samaritans.)
verseByVerse.commentary: The parenthetical explanation for Gentile readers (and the woman's own surprise) confirms that Jesus has crossed a major social boundary. The disciples' absence is providential: this conversation happens precisely because Jesus is alone. The woman's question is not hostile but genuinely puzzled — she has enough experience of Jewish contempt to be surprised by a Jewish request. Her surprise is the crack through which grace enters. When the wall of expected contempt does not appear, the heart opens a little, and Jesus speaks into that opening.

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus answered her, "If you knew the gift of God, and who it is that is saying to you, 'Give me a drink,' you would have asked him, and he would have given you living water."
verseByVerse.commentary: Jesus pivots from her water to his water, from his need to her need. If you knew — the condition points to the epistemological gap between them. She does not yet know who she is speaking with, and that ignorance is her poverty. The gift of God: living water is not earned, not bartered, not purchased at the noon-hour well of ordinary religion — it is gift. The one asking for a drink is the one who can give what no well contains. This is the pattern of all evangelism: begin with the human's ordinary need, move to the divine gift that satisfies the need beneath the need.

verseByVerse.quote: The woman said to him, "Sir, you have nothing to draw water with, and the well is deep. Where do you get that living water? Are you greater than our father Jacob? He gave us the well and drank from it himself, as did his sons and his livestock."
verseByVerse.commentary: The woman is practically minded: he has no bucket. She invokes Jacob — their shared patriarch — to challenge his implied superiority. Are you greater than Jacob? It is one of the great dramatic ironies of the gospel: yes, infinitely greater. The one who created Jacob, who named Israel, who watched over the patriarchs in every generation stands before her asking for a drink. She is asking the right question without knowing how right it is. Jesus never rebukes these questions; he uses them as stepping stones toward revelation.
