And it is he who is speaking to you: the same revelation formula as John 4:26 to the Samaritan woman. Jesus identifies himself directly to those whose hearts are prepared to receive the disclosure. The one who sought the cast-out finds him and reveals himself.

verseByVerse.quote: He said, "Lord, I believe," and he worshiped him. Jesus said, "For judgment I came into this world, that those who do not see may see, and those who see may become blind."
verseByVerse.commentary: Lord, I believe — and he worshiped: the progression of the entire chapter compressed into three words and one action. He began knowing only a name; he ends in worship of the Lord. For judgment I came: not as the primary purpose (3:17) but as the inevitable consequence. The light that illuminates also exposes. The coming of Christ produces a division: those who acknowledge their blindness receive sight; those who insist on their sight are confirmed in blindness. The judgment is not imposed from outside but revealed from within: every person's response to Jesus is the disclosure of what their heart truly is.

verseByVerse.quote: Some of the Pharisees near him heard these things, and said to him, "Are we also blind?" Jesus said to them, "If you were blind, you would have no guilt; but now that you say, 'We see,' your guilt remains."
verseByVerse.commentary: If you were blind, you would have no guilt: if they lacked the light entirely, their rejection would be excusable. But they have had the light — Torah, temple, prophets, and now Jesus himself — and they have chosen not to see. Culpable blindness is the blindness of those who could see but will not. Your guilt remains: the word used for sin remaining is the same as John 20:23 for sins retained in judgment. The Pharisees' confident self-assessment — We see — is the very thing that seals their blindness. The only cure for this blindness is the humility that admits it, and that admission is itself a work of grace.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–21 — The Good Shepherd Lays Down His Life
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Using the extended metaphor of shepherd, sheep, sheepfold, and hired hand, Jesus declares himself the door and the good shepherd. The discourse is addressed to the Pharisees who have just cast out the healed man (9:34), contrasting the true shepherd who lays down his life with the thieves, robbers, and hired hands who exploit or abandon the flock. The chapter's first half closes with another division among the crowd.
verseByVerse.theology: The shepherd imagery draws on the entire Old Testament tradition: God as shepherd (Ps. 23; Ezek. 34), the coming Davidic shepherd-king (Ezek. 34:23-24; Jer. 23:4), and the contrast between true and false shepherds throughout the prophets. Jesus claims all of these simultaneously: he is the door (the only legitimate access to God), the good shepherd (who gives rather than takes), and the one who lays down his life voluntarily (the self-giving that no hired hand would perform). The death is central: the shepherd metaphor cannot be understood apart from the cross.
verseByVerse.examples: The sheep hear his voice: the recognition of Christ by the elect is not achievement but gift. The sheep do not learn to recognize the shepherd's voice; they already know it because they are his sheep. This is Calvinist soteriology rendered in pastoral imagery: election precedes hearing, calling brings the elect home, and not one of the Father's sheep is lost. The Pharisees cannot hear because they are not sheep (v. 26); the church hears because she has been given ears by the Shepherd himself.

verseByVerse.quote: "Truly, truly, I say to you, he who does not enter the sheepfold by the door but climbs in by another way, that man is a thief and a robber. But he who enters by the door is the shepherd of the sheep."
verseByVerse.commentary: The sheepfold image would be immediately intelligible to a Palestinian audience: a stone enclosure where sheep were kept overnight, with a single door guarded by a doorkeeper or by the shepherd himself. Climbing in another way — avoiding the door — marks the thief. This verse indicts all who claim to speak for God while bypassing the appointed way of covenant authority: false prophets, self-appointed teachers, religious entrepreneurs who exploit rather than serve. Legitimate authority follows legitimate entry; the shepherd comes through the door because the door belongs to him by right.

verseByVerse.quote: "To him the gatekeeper opens. The sheep hear his voice, and he calls his own sheep by name and leads them out. When he has brought out all his own, he goes before them, and the sheep follow him, for they know his voice."
verseByVerse.commentary: He calls his own sheep by name: not anonymous management of a herd but personal, individual knowledge. The shepherd knows each sheep with the intimacy that names express — this is the pastoral counterpart to the Father's knowing of the elect by name before the foundation of the world. He goes before them: the shepherd does not drive the sheep from behind but leads from the front, walking into the danger first. The sheep follow because they know his voice — a knowledge that is not acquired skill but Spirit-given recognition, the 'hearing' that is the mark of the elect throughout this discourse.

verseByVerse.quote: "A stranger they will not follow, but they will flee from him, for they do not know the voice of strangers." This figure of speech Jesus used with them, but they did not understand what he was saying to them.
verseByVerse.commentary: The sheep discern voices — a spiritual discernment that protects from counterfeit shepherds. The stranger's voice does not ring true to ears tuned to the true shepherd. This is the practical function of the doctrine of Scripture: the sheep who know the Shepherd's voice in the written word can recognize when preachers contradict it. They did not understand: the Pharisees, who have just cast out the man who heard and followed Jesus, cannot grasp the parable that explains their own spiritual condition. They are not sheep; they are the strangers from whom the sheep flee.

verseByVerse.quote: So Jesus again said to them, "Truly, truly, I say to you, I am the door of the sheep. All who came before me are thieves and robbers, but the sheep did not listen to them."
verseByVerse.commentary: I am the door: the second great I AM of the chapter, and a different metaphor from the shepherd — now Jesus is the access point itself. The only legitimate entry into the sheepfold (the community of God's people, eternal life, the Father) is through Jesus. All who came before me as thieves: not the prophets (who all pointed forward to Jesus) but the false messianic pretenders and exploitative religious leaders who used spiritual authority for personal gain. The sheep's spiritual instinct protected them from these — the elect are not ultimately deceived by counterfeits.

verseByVerse.quote: "I am the door. If anyone enters by me, he will be saved and will go in and out and find pasture. The thief comes only to steal and kill and destroy. I came that they may have life and have it abundantly."
verseByVerse.commentary: I came that they may have life and have it abundantly: one of the great statements of the gospel's positive purpose. The contrast with the thief's agenda — steal, kill, destroy — defines what the enemy does to human souls and what the Shepherd came to undo. Abundant life is not prosperity-gospel plenty but the fullness of the life of God, the comprehensive shalom of the covenant that includes forgiveness, relationship, purpose, community, and the hope of resurrection. This is the positive side of the atonement: not merely rescue from death but gift of life, not merely pardon but adoption, not merely forgiveness but inheritance.

verseByVerse.quote: "I am the good shepherd. The good shepherd lays down his life for the sheep. He who is a hired hand and not a shepherd, who does not own the sheep, sees the wolf coming and leaves the sheep and flees, and the wolf snatches them and scatters them."
verseByVerse.commentary: The good shepherd lays down his life: the defining act that distinguishes the good shepherd from every imitation. The hired hand's failure is rooted in ownership: he does not own the sheep, so their loss is not his loss. The good shepherd owns the sheep — they are his, given to him by the Father (v. 29) — and therefore their safety is his personal concern. He will not flee because he cannot abandon what is his. The cross is not an external imposition on Jesus but the voluntary act of the owner who would rather die than lose one of his own.

verseByVerse.quote: "He flees because he is a hired hand and cares nothing for the sheep. I am the good shepherd. I know my own and my own know me."
verseByVerse.commentary: I know my own and my own know me: the mutual knowledge that defines the covenant relationship between Christ and his people. The Greek verb ginosko carries the weight of intimate, personal, relational knowledge — the knowledge of a shepherd who knows each sheep by name, and of sheep who have learned to distinguish the true voice from all others. This mutual knowing is patterned on (v. 15) the mutual knowing of the Father and Son: the intimacy within the Trinity becomes the model for the intimacy between Christ and the church. The sheep know the Shepherd because the Shepherd first knew them.

verseByVerse.quote: "just as the Father knows me and I know the Father; and I lay down my life for the sheep. And I have other sheep that are not of this fold. I must bring them also, and they will listen to my voice. So there will be one flock, one shepherd."
verseByVerse.commentary: Other sheep not of this fold: the Gentile mission announced in advance by the Shepherd himself. The boundary of Israel was never God's final boundary; from Abraham the promise was always 'in you all the nations will be blessed.' One flock, one shepherd: the eschatological unity of the people of God across every ethnic, linguistic, and national boundary. There will be no Jewish church and Gentile church, no first-class and second-class disciples — one flock under one Shepherd. This is the vision the book of Acts describes and the book of Revelation celebrates.

verseByVerse.quote: "For this reason the Father loves me, because I lay down my life that I may take it up again. No one takes it from me, but I lay it down of my own accord. I have authority to lay it down, and I have authority to take it up again. This charge I have received from my Father."
verseByVerse.commentary: No one takes it from me: the most explicit statement of the voluntary nature of the atonement. The enemies who arrest, try, and crucify Jesus are not the cause of his death; they are the instruments through which his own sovereign self-giving operates. He has authority to lay down and take up his life — a double authority that no human being possesses. The resurrection is not rescue from an unexpected catastrophe; it is the second act of the same sovereign will that freely laid down its life. The Father's love for the Son is expressed in this very willingness: the Son who lays down and takes up his life perfectly fulfills the Father's redemptive will.

verseByVerse.quote: There was again a division among the Jews because of these words. Many of them said, "He has a demon, and is insane; why listen to him?"
verseByVerse.commentary: Division again — the invariable result of Jesus' presence. The anti-party reaches for the stock accusation: demon, madness. This is how the fallen mind processes a claim that exceeds its categories: rather than revise the categories, dismiss the claimant as irrational or diabolical. The words of Jesus are either the sanest words ever spoken or the words of a lunatic or a liar — C.S. Lewis's trilemma applies here exactly. The crowd that says "why listen to him?" has made a choice, but it is not a neutral one; it is the choice of those who prefer their current darkness to the disruptive light.

verseByVerse.quote: Others said, "These are not the words of someone who is demon-possessed. Can a demon open the eyes of the blind?"
verseByVerse.commentary: The pro-party has an argument that cannot be answered: demonic power does not heal, it destroys. The opening of congenitally blind eyes is the work of the Creator, not the Adversary. Every authentic healing Jesus performs is an argument against the demonic-attribution hypothesis. The miracle of chapter 9 continues to exercise its evidential weight into chapter 10: healed eyes are facts that persist beyond the controversy they generated. The crowd's question — Can a demon do this? — is rhetorical, but it is also the right question. The answer, which the opposition cannot provide, is no.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 22–42 — I and the Father Are One
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: At the Feast of Dedication (Hanukkah), the Jews press Jesus for a direct statement: 'Are you the Christ?' Jesus answers by reference to his works and his relationship with the Father, declares 'I and the Father are one,' and survives another stoning attempt. He then withdraws beyond the Jordan where many believe in him.
verseByVerse.theology: The climactic declaration — I and the Father are one — is the theological summit of the Good Shepherd discourse and of John's presentation of Jesus' identity in the public ministry. The unity is not merely unity of purpose (though it includes that) but ontological unity — the unity of shared divine nature that the Jews correctly understand as a claim to deity (v. 33). Jesus defends the claim not by retreating from it but by appealing to the greater logic: if Scripture can call judges 'gods,' how much more can the one the Father consecrated and sent be called the Son of God? The defense is not a reduction of the claim but an escalation of it.
verseByVerse.examples: Beyond the Jordan, many believe on the basis of John's testimony confirmed by Jesus' works. This is the pattern of fruitful ministry: the faithful witness of the forerunner, confirmed by the reality of the one the forerunner announced, produces lasting faith. The chapter ends not in Jerusalem with hostility but in the wilderness with harvest — a reminder that the gospel often bears its richest fruit outside the centers of established religion.

verseByVerse.quote: At that time the Feast of Dedication took place at Jerusalem. It was winter, and Jesus was walking in the temple, in the colonnade of Solomon.
verseByVerse.commentary: The Feast of Dedication — Hanukkah — commemorated the Maccabean rededication of the temple in 164 BC after Antiochus Epiphanes IV had desecrated it by sacrificing a pig on the altar and erecting a statue of Zeus. When the Maccabees recaptured and cleansed the temple, they found only one cruse of ritually pure olive oil — enough to keep the great seven-branched menorah burning for a single day. According to the Talmud (Shabbat 21b), that oil burned miraculously for eight days — exactly the time needed to prepare a fresh supply of consecrated oil. This is why Hanukkah became specifically known as the Festival of Lights and is observed with the kindling of eight candles over eight nights. Solomon's Colonnade, where Jesus is walking, was a covered portico on the east side of the temple mount, sheltered from the winter cold. John's contextual irony is precise: the Light of the world (8:12) is walking through the temple precincts during the Festival of Lights — the festival celebrating oil that burned beyond all natural supply. Jesus is the inexhaustible light the Hanukkah menorah pointed to: his light comes not from a cruse of oil that might run dry but from the eternal life of the Father. He is himself the true temple (2:21), the true rededication of the sacred to God, the light that the darkness has never overcome (1:5).

verseByVerse.quote: So the Jews gathered around him and said to him, "How long will you keep us in suspense? If you are the Christ, tell us plainly." Jesus answered them, "I told you, and you do not believe. The works that I do in my Father's name bear witness about me."
verseByVerse.commentary: Tell us plainly: the demand for a straight answer, which sounds reasonable, is actually a demand for a confession they can use as a charge. They want a 'yes' they can bring to the authorities as blasphemy. Jesus' answer — I told you, and you do not believe — is not evasion but exposure: the problem is not insufficient information but the refusal of what has already been given. The works bear witness: the evidential trail is complete. More words will not produce belief where the works have not; the issue is not the adequacy of the evidence but the disposition of the heart.

verseByVerse.quote: "but you do not believe because you are not among my sheep. My sheep hear my voice, and I know them, and they follow me."
verseByVerse.commentary: You do not believe because you are not among my sheep: the most explicit statement of the election-before-faith sequence in the gospel. They are not lacking faith because they have not yet heard; they cannot hear because they are not sheep. The capacity to recognize the Shepherd's voice is not a universal human faculty but a Spirit-given gift to those who are the Father's gift to the Son. This is not fatalism but the pastoral realism of grace: the Shepherd knows his own; the question for every hearer is whether the voice of Jesus is recognizable — whether the Spirit has been given to open the ears.

verseByVerse.quote: "I give them eternal life, and they will never perish, and no one will snatch them out of my hand. My Father, who has given them to me, is greater than all, and no one is able to snatch them out of the Father's hand."
verseByVerse.commentary: The double security of the believer: held in the Son's hand and in the Father's hand simultaneously. No one can snatch them: the passive is universal — no force, human or demonic, external or internal, can remove the sheep from this double grip. The security is not the sheep's grip on the Shepherd but the Shepherd's grip on the sheep. This is the Reformed doctrine of the perseverance of the saints stated with maximum simplicity: they persevere because they are preserved, and they are preserved because the one who holds them is greater than all. No sheep the Father gave to the Son has ever been lost, and none ever will be.

verseByVerse.quote: "I and the Father are one." The Jews picked up stones again to stone him.
verseByVerse.commentary: I and the Father are one: seven words that contain the christological center of the fourth gospel. The unity is not merely ethical (we agree on all things) but ontological (we share the one divine nature). The Jews understand this immediately: they reach for stones. They are not misreading him. They correctly hear a claim to divine equality and respond with the law's penalty for blasphemy (Lev. 24:16). For the Christian reading this passage on the other side of Nicaea and Chalcedon, this verse is the scriptural anchor for the Trinitarian theology that the church has confessed since: one God in three persons, the Father and Son of one substance.

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus answered them, "I have shown you many good works from the Father; for which of them are you going to stone me?" The Jews answered him, "It is not for a good work that we are going to stone you but for blasphemy, because you, being a man, make yourself God."
verseByVerse.commentary: You, being a man, make yourself God: their charge is accurate and their penalty is specified in the law. What they cannot accept is the claim's truth. Jesus inverts the accusation: he is not a man claiming to be God but God who has become man — the direction is opposite. The stoning attempt for blasphemy is the legal mechanism by which the crucifixion will eventually operate: the charge at the trial will be the same (19:7). The authorities are building their case; Jesus is allowing them time to demonstrate the depth of their rejection. Every move toward the cross is simultaneously a move toward the resurrection that vindicates every claim they deny.

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus answered them, "Is it not written in your Law, 'I said, you are gods'? If he called them gods to whom the word of God came — and Scripture cannot be broken —"
verseByVerse.commentary: The argument from Psalm 82:6 — where judges are called "gods" because they exercise divine authority in God's name — operates a fortiori: if derivative, functional divine language can be applied to human judges by Scripture, the Scripture's own authority is the foundation (Scripture cannot be broken). Jesus uses the text against those who claim to honor it, demonstrating that their outrage is selective: they accept the language when applied to human judges but reject it when applied to the one the Father actually consecrated. The inerrancy of Scripture is here the fulcrum of the argument.

verseByVerse.quote: "do you say of him whom the Father consecrated and sent into the world, 'You are blaspheming,' because I said, 'I am the Son of God'?"
verseByVerse.commentary: Consecrated and sent: the two verbs define the Son's relationship to the Father in the mission of redemption. Consecrated — set apart, as the high priest was set apart, as the temple was set apart — points to eternal election. Sent — commissioned into the world — points to the incarnation. How can the one the Father himself consecrated and sent blaspheme by claiming the status that the consecration and sending confer? The charge of blasphemy assumes that Jesus is claiming unauthorized status; Jesus' defense is that the authorization is the most complete possible: the Father himself. The argument is unanswerable on its own terms.

verseByVerse.quote: "If I am not doing the works of my Father, then do not believe me; but if I do them, even though you do not believe me, believe the works, that you may know and understand that the Father is in me and I am in the Father."
verseByVerse.commentary: Believe the works: Jesus offers an empirical test — evaluate the works against the claim. If the claim is false, the works should not be possible. The works are themselves arguments for the mutual indwelling of Father and Son: that the Father is in me and I am in the Father. The mutual indwelling (perichoresis in later Trinitarian theology) is the inner-Trinitarian reality that produces the Son's works in the world. You cannot believe me, then believe the works — an act of gracious condescension: use whatever entry point you can find, just come to the truth. Jesus meets each person's capacity for faith wherever it begins.

verseByVerse.quote: Again they sought to arrest him, but he escaped from their hands. He went away again across the Jordan to the place where John had been baptizing at first, and there he remained.
verseByVerse.commentary: He escaped from their hands: not by miraculous teleportation but by the sovereign timing of the Father — the hour has not come. Jesus withdraws to the place of John's ministry at the beginning — the Jordan crossing, the threshold space — and remains there. The geography is retreat for renewal, not defeat. The ministry that began in public proclamation in Jerusalem will end in Jerusalem, but between the controversies Jesus withdraws to the places of beginning. Every sustained ministry requires times of withdrawal from the center of conflict to the places where the work first started and faith is simpler.

verseByVerse.quote: And many came to him. And they said, "John did no sign, but everything that John said about this man was true." And many believed in him there.
verseByVerse.commentary: Everything John said about this man was true: the Baptist's ministry, concluded years before, is now being vindicated by the people who heard it and now see its fulfillment. John did no sign — his witness was entirely verbal and confessional — but his words were accurate. Faithful verbal witness, even without miraculous confirmation, produces durable fruit. The people of the Jordan region believed Jesus not on the basis of signs alone but on the confirmed truth of John's testimony. Many believed there — outside Jerusalem, in the wilderness, among the people John had baptized. The harvest that Jerusalem refused, the margins received.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–44 — Lazarus Raised: The Sign That Decides
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The raising of Lazarus is the climactic sign of the fourth gospel, the seventh and greatest miracle, the one that crystallizes both faith (Mary, Martha, the disciples) and murderous opposition (the Sanhedrin's decision to kill Jesus, v. 53). Jesus allows a two-day delay that ensures Lazarus is undeniably dead before he arrives, then raises him with a word — a sign so overwhelming that it forces a decision: believe or destroy.
verseByVerse.theology: The miracle is a preview of Jesus' own resurrection and, through his, the resurrection of all who are in him. I am the resurrection and the life (v. 25) is not merely a claim about what Jesus can do but about what he is: the source and substance of resurrection-life, the one in whom the age-to-come has already broken into the present. Those who believe in him will never die — not because they avoid physical death but because they have already passed from death to life (5:24). Lazarus' resurrection is the bodily demonstration of what Jesus gives spiritually to every believer.
verseByVerse.examples: The weeping of Jesus (vv. 33-35) is one of the most theologically dense moments in the gospel: the one who knows he is about to raise Lazarus weeps with those who grieve. His tears are not ignorance of the outcome but solidarity with human grief, genuine compassion that does not remove itself from suffering even when it is about to overcome suffering. This is the incarnation at its most moving: God in the flesh does not observe human sorrow from a distance; he enters it, feels it, and weeps in it — before he conquers it.

verseByVerse.quote: Now a certain man was ill, Lazarus of Bethany, the village of Mary and her sister Martha. It was Mary who anointed the Lord with ointment and wiped his feet with her hair, whose brother Lazarus was ill.
verseByVerse.commentary: Lazarus of Bethany: a specific person, known by name, in a specific village with known sisters. The incarnation insists on particularity — grace comes to specific people in specific places with specific stories. John identifies Mary by her anointing of Jesus (12:3), proleptic identification that ties the death of Lazarus to the anointing that anticipates Jesus' own burial. The beloved family is introduced under the shadow of illness: love and suffering are inseparable in the world the gospel addresses, and Jesus' response to both will define his character and his mission.

verseByVerse.quote: So the sisters sent to him, saying, "Lord, he whom you love is ill." When Jesus heard it he said, "This illness does not lead to death. It leads to the glory of God, so that the Son of God may be glorified through it."
verseByVerse.commentary: He whom you love is ill: the appeal is to relationship, not formula. They do not ask for a specific outcome; they simply report the need to the one who loves. This is the perfect model of prayer: bringing the need to the one who cares, without prescribing the solution. This illness does not lead to death: not a denial that Lazarus will die (he will) but a statement about the final destination — the glory of God, not death. Every suffering that the sovereign Lord oversees has a destination beyond itself. The illness leads not to the last word of death but to the first word of resurrection glory.

verseByVerse.quote: Now Jesus loved Martha and her sister and Lazarus. So, when he heard that Lazarus was ill, he stayed two days longer in the place where he was.
verseByVerse.commentary: So, when he heard that Lazarus was ill, he stayed two days: the conjunction 'so' (oun) is the most startling word in the verse. Because Jesus loved them, he stayed. Divine love does not always look like immediate response; sometimes it looks like deliberate delay that serves a deeper purpose. The two-day delay ensures that Lazarus will be four days dead before Jesus arrives (v. 39) — beyond any possibility of natural resuscitation. The delay is the setup for the greatest sign. Love that seems absent is often love preparing the most magnificent display of itself.

verseByVerse.quote: Then after this he said to the disciples, "Let us go to Judea again." The disciples said to him, "Rabbi, the Jews were just now seeking to stone you, and are you going there again?"
verseByVerse.commentary: Let us go to Judea: the disciples immediately recall the stoning attempt of 10:31. The journey to Lazarus is simultaneously the journey toward the cross; Bethany is two miles from Jerusalem, and this return trip will set in motion the events that lead to Calvary. The disciples' concern is rational — the last visit to Judea nearly ended in stoning. Jesus' answer will frame the decision in terms of day and night, of the Father's appointed time. He does not deny the danger; he places the danger within the larger framework of sovereign timing that makes the danger, in the end, no threat at all.

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus answered, "Are there not twelve hours in the day? If anyone walks in the day, he does not stumble, because he sees the light of this world. But if anyone walks in the night, he stumbles, because the light is not in him."
verseByVerse.commentary: Twelve hours of daylight: the appointed time for work and walking. Jesus operates within the day the Father has given him — while the light lasts, while his hour is not yet come. The one who walks in the day does not stumble; the one who walks in the night does. Jesus is the light of the world; walking in his presence is walking in the light that eliminates stumbling. For the disciples, following Jesus to Judea is not reckless courage but light-directed obedience: the Light is going; following the Light is the safest path, however dangerous it looks by the world's reckoning.

verseByVerse.quote: After saying these things, he said to them, "Our friend Lazarus has fallen asleep, but I go to awaken him." The disciples said to him, "Lord, if he has fallen asleep, he will recover."
verseByVerse.commentary: Fallen asleep: Jesus uses the language of sleep for death — not euphemism but theological claim. Death for those who are in Christ is sleep, a temporary rest from which they will be awakened. The disciples hear literally and respond literally: good, then he'll recover on his own, no need to risk Judea. They consistently read the physical level of Jesus' speech and miss the spiritual. This is not stupidity but the characteristic failure of those who have not yet been illuminated by the Spirit: the natural mind cannot receive the things of the Spirit of God (1 Cor. 2:14).

verseByVerse.quote: Now Jesus had spoken of his death, but they thought that he meant taking rest in sleep. So Jesus told them plainly, "Lazarus has died."
verseByVerse.commentary: Jesus told them plainly: when the metaphor fails, he speaks directly. Lazarus has died. The plain speech is harder than the metaphor; death is death, and the disciples must face it without softening. Jesus does not protect his followers from the hard truths but waits until they are necessary and then speaks them clearly. The move from metaphor to plain speech is also a move toward the disciples' deeper understanding — and toward the journey that will demonstrate what plainly-stated death means in the hands of the resurrection and the life.

verseByVerse.quote: "and for your sake I am glad that I was not there, so that you may believe. But let us go to him." So Thomas, called the Twin, said to his fellow disciples, "Let us also go, that we may die with him."
verseByVerse.commentary: For your sake I am glad: the delay that seemed like absence was actually for the disciples' benefit — to produce a faith deeper than what a bedside healing could generate. Thomas's response — let us go and die with him — is part loyalty and part fatalism: he expects the Jerusalem visit to end in execution. His courage, however tinged with despair, is real. He will go. This is imperfect faith at its best: uncertain of the outcome, fearful of the cost, but following anyway. Jesus does not wait for perfect faith before accepting it; he works with what is offered and refines it along the way.

verseByVerse.quote: Now when Jesus came, he found that Lazarus had already been in the tomb four days. Bethany was near Jerusalem, about two miles off.
verseByVerse.commentary: Four days in the tomb: the rabbinical tradition held that the soul departed the body after three days (when decomposition became visible). Four days removes every possibility of natural resuscitation; Lazarus is undeniably, irrevocably dead. The proximity to Jerusalem — two miles — ensures that the miracle will be public and will reach the authorities immediately. The raising of Lazarus is not performed in private; it happens in the full view of mourning Jerusalem, with witnesses from the city present (v. 31, 45). The sign cannot be hidden; it is designed to force a decision.

verseByVerse.quote: and many of the Jews had come to Martha and Mary to console them concerning their brother. So when Martha heard that Jesus was coming, she went and met him, while Mary remained seated in the house.
verseByVerse.commentary: The two sisters respond characteristically: Martha goes out to meet Jesus (active, confrontational in the best sense), while Mary remains in the house (contemplative, weighted with grief). Neither response is wrong; both will receive what they need. The crowd of mourners from Jerusalem will become witnesses to the greatest sign — providentially gathered for consolation, they will see resurrection. Human mourning becomes the context for divine glory. God uses our ordinary responses to grief as the occasion for his extraordinary self-disclosure.

verseByVerse.quote: Martha said to Jesus, "Lord, if you had been here, my brother would not have died. But even now I know that whatever you ask from God, God will give you."
verseByVerse.commentary: Lord, if you had been here: the grief-inflected if is not accusation but confession of faith in his power. Martha believes Jesus could have prevented the death; she does not understand yet that he can undo it. But even now: the qualifying phrase that opens the door to something more. She does not know what she is asking for, but her 'even now' expresses a faith in Jesus' ongoing relationship with God that goes beyond the specific request. This is intercessory faith in its early form: more than human comfort can provide, less than resurrection expectation — but oriented in the right direction.

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus said to her, "Your brother will rise again." Martha said to him, "I know that he will rise again in the resurrection on the last day."
verseByVerse.commentary: Your brother will rise again: Jesus' promise is deliberately ambiguous, and Martha hears it in the most conventional sense: the general resurrection at the end of history. Her theology is correct and orthodox — the Pharisaic resurrection hope. But Jesus is about to collapse the eschatological future into the present: not the last day but today, not the general resurrection but a specific resurrection that prefigures and guarantees the general one. Martha's faith is real but limited to the categories she has. Jesus is about to expand those categories beyond anything she can imagine.

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus said to her, "I am the resurrection and the life. Whoever believes in me, though he die, yet shall he live, and everyone who lives and believes in me shall never die. Do you believe this?"
verseByVerse.commentary: I am the resurrection and the life: not 'I will bring resurrection' or 'I teach about resurrection' but I am — the resurrection is located in his person, not in a future event. The fifth great I AM saying of the gospel is its most comprehensive claim: he is the source and substance of all resurrection-life. Whoever believes in me, though he die, yet shall he live: physical death cannot terminate the life received from Jesus. Everyone who lives and believes in me shall never die: spiritual death has no power over those who are in him. Do you believe this? — the question presses every listener to personal decision. Christology is always invitation.

verseByVerse.quote: She said to him, "Yes, Lord; I believe that you are the Christ, the Son of God, who is coming into the world." When she had said this, she went and called her sister Mary, saying in private, "The Teacher is here and is calling for you."
verseByVerse.commentary: Martha's confession — Christ, Son of God, the one coming into the world — is the gospel's full christological formula. The Evangelist has been building to exactly this throughout the book (20:31). Like Peter's confession (Matt. 16:16), Martha's confession is elicited by Jesus' own question and goes beyond what she can yet fully comprehend. She believes who he is before she sees what he will do. This is the order of grace: confession of Christ precedes experience of his full power. And immediately: she goes to share the news with her sister. The one who has heard the call to belief immediately brings others to hear the same call.

verseByVerse.quote: And when she heard it, she rose quickly and went to him. Now Jesus had not yet come into the village, but was still in the place where Martha had met him.
verseByVerse.commentary: She rose quickly: the urgency of love responding to the call of the one she loves. Mary's movement toward Jesus mirrors the soul's response to the gospel call — not leisurely weighing of options but immediate, undelayed response to the summons. Jesus remains outside the village, holding his position at the threshold. He will not force his way into the grief; he waits to be summoned, to be received, to enter where he is wanted. This is the pattern of grace: offered, not imposed; available, not coercive. He stands at the door and knocks.

verseByVerse.quote: When the Jews who were with her in the house, consoling her, saw Mary rise quickly and go out, they followed her, supposing that she was going to the tomb to weep there. Therefore, when Mary came to where Jesus was and saw him, she fell at his feet, saying to him, "Lord, if you had been here, my brother would not have died."
verseByVerse.commentary: The mourners follow Mary — and thereby become witnesses to the greatest sign. Providence arranges the witness-list through the ordinary movements of grief: they follow because they think she is going to weep, and they find something that will give them something greater to weep about and then something infinitely better to rejoice in. Mary falls at his feet — the posture of worship and of grief simultaneously. Her words echo Martha's exactly, but the emotional register is different: where Martha was composed, Mary is weeping. Jesus receives both responses with the same perfect compassion.

verseByVerse.quote: When Jesus therefore saw her weeping, and the Jews who came with her also weeping, he was deeply moved in his spirit and greatly troubled. And he said, "Where have you laid him?" They said to him, "Lord, come and see."
verseByVerse.commentary: Deeply moved in his spirit and greatly troubled: the Greek (embrimaomai) suggests a strong emotional response — some translate it as anger, some as deep distress, some as righteous indignation at death itself. Jesus is moved by the sight of grief; he does not observe it from a safe emotional distance. The one who is about to conquer death first weeps with those death has wounded. This is the incarnation at its most tender: the omnipotent one troubled, the sovereign one moved, the eternal one entering into the anguish of the temporal. Come and see: the same words Philip said to Nathanael (1:46), now said to God incarnate.

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus wept. So the Jews said, "See how he loved him!"
verseByVerse.commentary: Jesus wept: the shortest verse in the English Bible and one of the most theologically profound. He who knows the outcome — he is about to reverse it — still weeps. His tears are not ignorance or despair but love: he loved Lazarus, he loved Mary, he loved Martha, and love weeps with the weeping. The crowd draws the right inference: see how he loved him. The incarnation means that God's love for the world is not abstract benevolence but particular, personal affection that expresses itself in tears. The God who does not weep is not the God of the Bible; the God who weeps with us before he defeats for us is the God of the gospel.

verseByVerse.quote: But some of them said, "Could not he who opened the eyes of the blind man also have kept this man from dying?" So Jesus, deeply moved again, came to the tomb. It was a cave, and a stone lay against it.
verseByVerse.commentary: Could not he who opened the blind man's eyes have prevented this? The question is not hostile but agonized — the grief of those who believe in Jesus' power but cannot understand his timing. It is the question of every believer who prays and is not immediately answered: if you can, why didn't you? Jesus receives the question without explanation, deeply moved again — the same word as verse 33 — and goes to the tomb. Sometimes the answer to the question of suffering is not an explanation but a presence: God coming to where the grief is and acting in a way that transforms the question.

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus said, "Take away the stone." Martha, the sister of the dead man, said to him, "Lord, by this time there will be an odor, for he has been dead four days." Jesus said to her, "Did I not tell you that if you believed you would see the glory of God?"
verseByVerse.commentary: Take away the stone: the command is simple, practical, and breathtaking in its expectation. Martha's objection — the smell of four-day decomposition — is medically accurate and theologically inadequate. She is thinking within the constraints of the natural order; Jesus is operating outside them. Did I not tell you: a gentle but firm recall to his earlier promise. If you believed you would see the glory of God: the condition is not achievement-faith but receptive-faith, the faith that takes Jesus at his word and acts on what he has said. The stone is an obstacle that human obedience can remove; what lies behind the stone requires divine power.

verseByVerse.quote: So they took away the stone. And Jesus lifted up his eyes and said, "Father, I thank you that you have heard me. I know that you always hear me, but I said this on account of the people standing around, that they may believe that you sent me."
verseByVerse.commentary: The prayer of thanksgiving before the miracle: Jesus operates in constant communion with the Father; the raising of Lazarus is not a unilateral display of power but the Trinitarian work of Father and Son acting together. I know that you always hear me: the Son's confidence in the Father's hearing is absolute — not presumption but the certainty of eternal, perfect relationship. I said this for the people: the prayer is simultaneously communion with the Father and witness to the crowd. Everything Jesus does serves the double purpose of honoring the Father and revealing the Father's love to the world.

verseByVerse.quote: When he had said these things, he cried out with a loud voice, "Lazarus, come out." The man who had died came out, his hands and feet bound with linen strips, and his face wrapped with a cloth. Jesus said to them, "Unbind him, and let him go."
verseByVerse.commentary: Lazarus, come out: three words that undo four days of death. The voice that called the universe into being calls Lazarus from the tomb. He comes out — still wrapped in burial cloths, barely able to move — a picture of the believer in the early stages of resurrection life: alive but not yet free. Unbind him, and let him go: the liberation from grave-clothes is the work of the community; the resurrection itself is the work of Christ alone. The church cannot give life — only Christ can do that — but the church can unbind: help people leave behind the habits and bondages that the old life left on them even after new life has come.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 45–57 — The Decision to Kill Jesus
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The raising of Lazarus produces the final polarization: many believe, some report to the Pharisees, the Sanhedrin convenes and decides that Jesus must die. Caiaphas' unwitting prophecy — 'It is better for one man to die for the people' — is God's own redemptive purpose spoken through unbelieving lips. Jesus withdraws to Ephraim; the crowds gather for Passover and wonder if he will appear.
verseByVerse.theology: Caiaphas' political calculation — sacrifice one man to save the nation — is simultaneously cynical expediency and unconscious prophecy. John explicitly identifies it as prophecy (v. 51): the high priest, by virtue of his office, spoke better than he knew. The death he plots as preservation of institutional power is the death that will actually accomplish the salvation of God's people — and not only of the Jewish nation, but of the scattered children of God throughout the world (v. 52). The cross is always more than its perpetrators intend and exactly what God intends.
verseByVerse.examples: The decision of the Sanhedrin is the human side of the decree that was made in eternity: Christ was the Lamb slain before the foundation of the world (Rev. 13:8). Human hatred and divine love converge on the same event. The leaders plot what God has purposed; the victim goes willingly to what they intend as murder and he intends as sacrifice. The sovereign grace that works through human wickedness without being compromised by it is most visible at Calvary.

verseByVerse.quote: Many of the Jews therefore, who had come with Mary and had seen what he did, believed in him, but some of them went to the Pharisees and told them what Jesus had done.
verseByVerse.commentary: The same miracle, the same witnesses, two completely opposite responses: many believed, some reported. Grace is not irresistible in the sense of mechanical coercion; it is effective in those to whom the Father gives it and resisted in those to whom it is not given. The reporters are not necessarily hostile at this point — they may have been merely reporting an unusual event — but their report sets the machinery of opposition in motion. The witness of God's works always produces this dual response in a fallen world. The same resurrection that produces faith in some produces the determination to suppress the one who performed it in others.

verseByVerse.quote: So the chief priests and the Pharisees gathered the council and said, "What are we doing? For this man performs many signs. If we let him go on like this, everyone will believe in him, and the Romans will come and take away both our place and our nation."
verseByVerse.commentary: The Sanhedrin's agenda is institutional self-preservation. The signs are acknowledged — they cannot deny them — but the response to the signs is political calculation: if everyone believes in him, Rome will suppress a messianic movement and destroy what remains of Jewish autonomy. They are trading the true salvation of their people for the preservation of their institutional position. This is the perennial temptation of religious institutions: protecting the system at the cost of the substance, preserving the vessel while losing the treasure. They will lose both: the system falls in AD 70, and the salvation they rejected was the only one on offer.

verseByVerse.quote: But one of them, Caiaphas, who was high priest that year, said to them, "You know nothing at all. Nor do you understand that it is better for you that one man should die for the people, not that the whole nation should perish."
verseByVerse.commentary: Caiaphas cuts through the council's hand-wringing with ruthless political logic: one man's death for the nation's survival is an acceptable trade. It is realpolitik, not theology — the calculation of the professional politician who has learned to think in acceptable casualties. But John will immediately identify it as prophecy: the words are truer than Caiaphas knows, in a way he cannot imagine. The high priest who plots murder becomes the unwilling instrument of the truth he calculates cynically. Providence has a long history of putting prophetic words in the mouths of those who think they are only being practical.

verseByVerse.quote: He did not say this of his own accord, but being high priest that year he prophesied that Jesus would die for the nation, and not for the nation only, but also to gather into one the children of God who are scattered abroad.
verseByVerse.commentary: Being high priest that year he prophesied: the office carries anointing even when the occupant is corrupt. Caiaphas did not know he was prophesying; the Spirit used the high priestly office to announce what the sacrifice would accomplish. Not for the nation only: the atonement extends beyond Israel to gather the scattered children of God from every nation — the same prediction Jesus made about 'other sheep' (10:16). The death plotted as national political strategy is the event that will unite Jewish and Gentile believers in one people under one Shepherd. God consistently accomplishes through the malice of his enemies exactly what his love has purposed from eternity.

verseByVerse.quote: So from that day on they made plans to put him to death. Jesus therefore no longer walked openly among the Jews, but went from there to the region near the wilderness, to a town called Ephraim, and there he stayed with the disciples.
verseByVerse.commentary: From that day on they made plans to put him to death: the official decision has been taken. The Sanhedrin's conspiracy is now the framework within which Jesus moves — and he moves accordingly, withdrawing to Ephraim near the wilderness. Not from fear but from timing: his hour has not yet come, and he will not allow it to come before the Father appoints it. The wilderness at Ephraim echoes the wilderness of the Exodus — the place of preparation before the great crossing. Jesus is preparing his disciples for what is about to happen, holding the appointed time in his own hands.

verseByVerse.quote: Now the Passover of the Jews was at hand, and many went up from the country to Jerusalem before the Passover to purify themselves. They were looking for Jesus and saying to one another as they stood in the temple, "What do you think? That he will not come to the feast at all?"
verseByVerse.commentary: Passover preparations and the search for Jesus converge: the feast that celebrates the Exodus lamb is the feast at which the Lamb of God will be slain. The pilgrims who have come to purify themselves for Passover are about to witness the purification of the world through the death of the one Lamb whose blood actually cleanses. What do you think? — the crowd speculates about whether Jesus will appear. They do not know they are asking about the most consequential appearance in human history: the Lamb's final entry into Jerusalem to offer himself as the sacrifice that ends all sacrifices.

verseByVerse.quote: Now the chief priests and the Pharisees had given orders that if anyone knew where he was, he should let them know, so that they might arrest him.
verseByVerse.commentary: The official arrest warrant is outstanding. The authorities are hunting; Jesus is withdrawing and preparing. The machinery of human hostility is in motion; the divine timetable is still running on schedule. These two realities — human plotting and divine sovereignty — will intersect at Gethsemane, when Jesus, not the soldiers, takes the initiative (18:4-8). The one they are hunting will hand himself over at the moment of his own choosing, in his own way, on his Father's timetable. The arrest warrant is real, but the prisoner controls the timing of his own arrest. The Lamb goes willingly to the altar.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–19 — The Anointing and the Entry
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Mary anoints Jesus with costly perfume, anticipating his burial; Judas objects, revealing his true character; the crowd greets Jesus' triumphal entry while the Pharisees despair. These two events — intimate anointing and public procession — together frame the final week: the love of the devoted and the pretense of the institutional, the fragrance of sacrifice and the noise of misunderstood triumph.
verseByVerse.theology: Mary's extravagance is the gospel's aesthetic: 'she has done a beautiful thing' (Matt. 26:10). The ointment worth a year's wages poured out on Jesus is the only appropriate response to the one who will pour out his life for the world. Judas' objection — it should have been sold and given to the poor — sounds pious but is calculated. He uses the language of charity to mask the language of control. The contrast between Mary's love and Judas' calculation is the contrast between authentic discipleship and the discipleship that has never really left the world's economy.
verseByVerse.examples: The triumphal entry is at once a royal procession and a misunderstood one. The crowd hails Jesus as king; they are right about the title and wrong about what it means. They expect a Davidic warrior-king who will restore national sovereignty; Jesus enters on a donkey, fulfilling Zechariah 9:9, the prophecy of the humble king of peace. The disciples do not understand this until after the resurrection (v. 16) — another instance of John's pattern where events are incomprehensible until the Spirit illuminates them in the light of the cross and resurrection.

verseByVerse.quote: Six days before the Passover, Jesus therefore came to Bethany, where Lazarus was, whom Jesus had raised from the dead. So they gave a dinner for him there. Martha served, and Lazarus was one of those reclining with him at table.
verseByVerse.commentary: Six days before the Passover: John begins his countdown to the crucifixion. Bethany, the village of resurrection, is the last resting place before Jerusalem. The dinner is an act of gratitude and fellowship — Martha serving (characteristically active), Lazarus reclining at table (alive, eating, tangible evidence of what Jesus does). The household of Lazarus is the household of the already-resurrected, a preview of the community of the new creation: those who were dead and now live, eating with the one who will himself die and rise.

verseByVerse.quote: Mary therefore took a pound of expensive ointment made from pure nard, and anointed the feet of Jesus and wiped his feet with her hair. The house was filled with the fragrance of the ointment. But Judas Iscariot, one of his disciples (he who was about to betray him), said,
verseByVerse.commentary: The contrast is stark and immediate: Mary's act of extravagant love, Judas' identity as betrayer already established by John before the objection is heard. The ointment is nard — imported from the Himalayan mountains, worth three hundred denarii (nearly a year's wages). She anoints his feet and wipes them with her hair: the reversal of normal servitude, the abandonment of social dignity in an act of total devotion. The fragrance fills the house — grace has that quality, it cannot be contained, it spreads beyond the person who offers it. All present are caught in the sweet smell of sacrificial love.

verseByVerse.quote: "Why was this ointment not sold for three hundred denarii and given to the poor?" He said this, not because he cared about the poor, but because he was a thief, and having charge of the moneybag he used to help himself to what was put into it.
verseByVerse.commentary: John's editorial parenthesis is devastating in its precision: Judas did not care about the poor; he was a thief who helped himself to the common fund. The righteous-sounding objection — sell it for the poor — is moral laundering. This is the pattern of false discipleship: using the language of the gospel's values (care for the poor) to serve personal interest. It is particularly dangerous because it is indistinguishable from genuine concern without the diagnostic knowledge John here provides. The Lord who knows what is in man (2:25) knows the difference between the Judases and the Marys, even when their language overlaps.

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus said, "Leave her alone, so that she may keep it for the day of my burial. For the poor you always have with you, but you do not always have me."
verseByVerse.commentary: Leave her alone: Jesus defends Mary against Judas with a directness that is itself an act of protective love. Her action, which she may not have fully understood, has a meaning he does name: she has anointed him for burial. The fragrant ointment will linger in the house; the crucified body will receive its burial ointment from Nicodemus (19:39-40). But what Mary has done cannot be taken back. The poor you always have with you: not an indifference to poverty but a calibration of the unique and unrepeatable moment. There will be opportunities to serve the poor; there is only one moment to anoint the Son of God for his sacrificial death.

verseByVerse.quote: When the large crowd of the Jews learned that Jesus was there, they came, not only on account of him but also to see Lazarus, whom he had raised from the dead. So the chief priests made plans to put Lazarus to death as well, because on account of him many of the Jews were going away and believing in Jesus.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The crowd comes for two reasons: Jesus and Lazarus — the performer of miracles and the evidence of miracles. Living evidence is more compelling than testimony about past events. And so the institutional response to living evidence is to destroy it: the chief priests plan to kill Lazarus to eliminate the testimony. This is the logical endpoint of institutional unbelief: when the evidence cannot be answered, eliminate the evidence. The resurrection that was meant to produce faith has produced a murder plot against the resurrected man. The powers of death always try to reclaim what the power of life has liberated.

The faith spreading through the Lazarus testimony is the immediate cause of the intensification of the plot.

verseByVerse.quote: The next day the large crowd that had come to the feast heard that Jesus was coming to Jerusalem. So they took branches of palm trees and went out to meet him, crying out, "Hosanna! Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord, even the King of Israel!" And Jesus found a young donkey and sat on it, just as it is written,
verseByVerse.commentary:
The crowd that has come to Jerusalem for Passover hears that Jesus is coming: word travels fast in a city full of pilgrims who have been asking about him (11:56). The convergence of the Passover festival (thousands of pilgrims) and the raising of Lazarus (the most dramatic sign yet) creates the conditions for the public entry. Everything is moving toward the appointed moment — the hour that Jesus has been saying had not yet come is now very nearly here.

Palm branches were symbols of Jewish nationalism and victory — used at the rededication of the temple (Maccabees) and at the Festival of Tabernacles. The crowd greets Jesus as a conquering king: Hosanna (Save now!), Blessed is he who comes (Ps. 118:26), King of Israel. They are right about the title and wrong about the method. Jesus' response is to find not a warhorse but a donkey — the fulfillment of Zechariah 9:9, the prophet's vision of the humble king who makes peace. He accepts the acclamation but corrects the expectation through the animal he chooses.

verseByVerse.quote: "Fear not, daughter of Zion; behold, your king is coming, sitting on a donkey's colt!" His disciples did not understand these things at first, but when Jesus was glorified, then they remembered that these things had been written about him and had been done to him.
verseByVerse.commentary: His disciples did not understand these things at first: the honest admission that accompanies every major event in John's gospel. The triumphal entry made no sense to the disciples while it was happening — they did not grasp the donkey's significance or the prophecy's fulfillment. When Jesus was glorified: the resurrection and ascension were the hermeneutical event that made the past intelligible. Pentecost illuminated Passover; the resurrection decoded the entry. Christian memory is always retrospective: we understand what we participated in after the Spirit opens our eyes. This is why the church can say more about the Trinity than the disciples could say during Jesus' ministry.

verseByVerse.quote: The crowd that had been with him when he called Lazarus out of the tomb and raised him from the dead continued to bear witness. The reason why the crowd went to meet him was that they heard he had done this sign.
verseByVerse.commentary: The testimony about Lazarus is the engine driving the crowd. Two groups converge: those who witnessed the resurrection directly and continued to testify, and those who heard their testimony and came to see for themselves. This is the apostolic pattern: eyewitnesses testify, hearers believe, believers become witnesses. The chain of testimony from the tomb to the Passover crowd to the entire Mediterranean world to our generation is unbroken. We believe on the basis of testimony that originated with those who were there when the stone rolled away and Lazarus walked out.

verseByVerse.quote: So the Pharisees said to one another, "You see that you are gaining nothing. Look, the world has gone after him."
verseByVerse.commentary: The world has gone after him: the Pharisees' despairing complaint is ironic prophecy — in trying to suppress Jesus, they are witnessing the beginning of the world-mission that the cross and resurrection will unleash.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 20–50 — The Hour Has Come: Lifting Up the Son of Man
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Greeks come seeking Jesus, prompting the announcement that 'the hour has come.' Jesus speaks of the grain of wheat, the lifting up that will draw all people, the voice from heaven, and the crisis that his presence creates. The section concludes with a sustained reflection on unbelief and the light that has come into the world, closing out the public ministry.
verseByVerse.theology: The hour is the theological center of John's gospel — referenced as 'not yet come' repeatedly throughout the narrative (2:4; 7:30; 8:20), now announced as arrived (v. 23). The hour is the cross-resurrection-ascension event, the moment when the Son of Man is simultaneously lifted up in humiliation and glorified in triumph. The cross is not the Father's defeat but his decisive victory; it is not the Son's shame but his glory. This is the theology that has to be maintained against every attempt to split the crucifixion from the resurrection: both are the one event called 'the hour.'
verseByVerse.examples: Unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies, it remains alone; but if it dies, it bears much fruit. This is the law of the kingdom: life through death, fruitfulness through sacrifice. Jesus applies it first to himself and then to his disciples. The disciple who 'hates his life in this world' — who does not cling to temporal existence at the cost of eternal loyalty — will find life preserved in ways that the self-preserver never can. Bonhoeffer's formulation: 'When Christ calls a man, he bids him come and die.'

verseByVerse.quote: Now among those who went up to worship at the feast were some Greeks. So these came to Philip, who was from Bethsaida in Galilee, and asked him, "Sir, we wish to see Jesus."
verseByVerse.commentary: We wish to see Jesus: the request of every genuinely seeking soul in every generation. The Greeks — Gentile god-fearers who have come to Jerusalem for Passover — represent the world that exists outside the covenant community but has been drawn toward the God of Israel. They approach Philip, the disciple with a Greek name from the bilingual city of Bethsaida. Their request will prompt Jesus' announcement of the hour — the universal scope of the Gentile mission is the occasion for the disclosure of the cross. Seeing Jesus costs more than they know they are asking for; but what it costs is what it gives.

verseByVerse.quote: Philip went and told Andrew; Andrew and Philip went and told Jesus. And Jesus answered them, "The hour has come for the Son of Man to be glorified."
verseByVerse.commentary: The hour has come: the announcement the entire gospel has been building toward. The arrival of the Greeks — representatives of 'the world' that has 'gone after him' — signals the moment. The Son of Man is to be glorified: not the national Davidic king the crowd wanted, but the lifted-up Son of Man of Daniel 7 whose dominion extends to all peoples, nations, and languages. The glorification Jesus announces is the cross seen from the perspective of heaven: the moment when love's ultimate act is performed and the Father's saving purpose is accomplished. The hour that was 'not yet' is now.

verseByVerse.quote: "Truly, truly, I say to you, unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies, it remains alone; but if it dies, it bears much fruit. Whoever loves his life loses it, and whoever hates his life in this world will keep it for eternal life."
verseByVerse.commentary: The grain of wheat parable is Jesus' own interpretation of his coming death. Alone versus much fruit: the choice is between preservation that leads to barrenness and sacrifice that leads to multiplication. The same law applies to disciples: the one who clings to temporal life loses it; the one who releases it for Christ's sake receives it back in a way that cannot be taken. This is not masochism but kingdom economics: the currency of the new creation is not accumulation but sacrifice, not self-preservation but self-giving. Jesus models what he commands; he is himself the grain of wheat.

verseByVerse.quote: "If anyone serves me, he must follow me; and where I am, there will my servant be also. If anyone serves me, the Father will honor him. Now is my soul troubled. And what shall I say? 'Father, save me from this hour'? But for this purpose I have come to this hour."
verseByVerse.commentary: If anyone serves me, he must follow me: discipleship is not admiration from a distance but the path of the grain of wheat — death and fruitfulness, suffering and resurrection. Where I am, there will my servant be also: the servant shares the master's path, including the path of the cross and, through it, the path of resurrection glory. Now is my soul troubled: the Gethsemane-like realism of the moment — Jesus is not stoically indifferent to what approaches. But for this purpose I have come to this hour: the trouble does not produce retreat. The hour is not intrusion but fulfillment.

verseByVerse.quote: "Father, glorify your name." Then a voice came from heaven: "I have glorified it, and I will glorify it again." The crowd that stood there and heard it said that it had thundered. Others said, "An angel has spoken to him."
verseByVerse.commentary: Father, glorify your name: the prayer is not for rescue from the hour but for the Father's name to be glorified through it. The Father's answer comes from heaven — the third direct divine voice in Jesus' ministry (baptism, transfiguration, here) — affirming that the glorification has already begun (in Jesus' ministry) and will be completed (in the cross and resurrection). The crowd cannot agree on what they heard: thunder or angel? The voice of God sounds different depending on the spiritual condition of the listener. Those who are the Father's hear it as address; those who are not hear it as weather.

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus answered, "This voice has come for your sake, not mine. Now is the judgment of this world; now will the ruler of this world be cast out."
verseByVerse.commentary: The judgment of this world and the casting out of its ruler happen not at the final judgment but at the cross. The death of Jesus is simultaneously the condemnation of the world-system that operates under the devil's influence and the decisive defeat of the devil himself. Hebrews 2:14-15 explains it: through death Jesus destroyed the one who had the power of death. The cross appears to be the enemy's victory — he has arranged the execution of the Son of God — but it is in fact his defeat, the moment when the power of death is broken by the one who dies and rises. The hour of apparent defeat is the hour of actual triumph.

verseByVerse.quote: "And I, when I am lifted up from the earth, will draw all people to myself." He said this to show by what kind of death he was going to die.
verseByVerse.commentary: When I am lifted up: the ambiguity of crucifixion (lifted up on a cross) and exaltation (lifted up to glory) is deliberate — both are the same event seen from different angles. Will draw all people to myself: the universal scope of the atonement's drawing power. Not all without exception will respond, but the cross's magnetic force reaches across every boundary — ethnic, cultural, historical — drawing those the Father gives to the Son from every tribe and language and people and nation. The cross does not merely make salvation possible; it actively draws. The drawing is the Spirit's work through the proclamation of the crucified and risen Lord.

verseByVerse.quote: So the crowd answered him, "We have heard from the Law that the Christ remains forever. How can you say that the Son of Man must be lifted up? Who is this Son of Man?" So Jesus said to them, "The light is among you for a little while longer. Walk while you have the light, lest darkness overtake you. The one who walks in the darkness does not know where he is going."
verseByVerse.commentary: The crowd's theological objection is real: if the Messiah remains forever, how can he be lifted up in death? They understand the finality of death but not the reality of resurrection — or the way that the 'being lifted up' is the pathway to the eternal reign, not its contradiction. Jesus does not resolve the paradox with argument; he responds with urgency: the light is present now; walk in it while you have it. The time for deliberation is running out. The darkness that follows the departure of the Light is disorienting in a way that those who have always lived in the dark cannot anticipate.

verseByVerse.quote: "While you have the light, believe in the light, that you may become sons of light." When Jesus had said these things, he departed and hid himself from them. Though he had done so many signs before them, they still did not believe in him,
verseByVerse.commentary: Sons of light: the goal of believing in the Light is not merely receiving illumination but being transformed into children of light — those who bear the family resemblance of the Father of lights. Jesus departs and hides: the withdrawal of the light creates darkness, which is itself a judgment on those who refused the light while it was available. They still did not believe — after the signs, after the teaching, after the raising of Lazarus. The inability to believe is not the excuse of insufficient evidence but the verdict of hearts that have hardened against the evidence they have received.

verseByVerse.quote: so that the word spoken by the prophet Isaiah might be fulfilled: "Lord, who has believed what he heard from us, and to whom has the arm of the Lord been revealed?" Therefore they could not believe. For again Isaiah said,
verseByVerse.commentary: Isaiah 53:1 — the suffering servant chapter — is cited to explain mass unbelief: who has believed our report? The question presupposes that many will not. The prophets anticipated the rejection; the rejection fulfills the prophecy. Therefore they could not believe: the inability is judicial, not mechanical — God has confirmed them in the hardness they have chosen. The arm of the Lord revealed is the gospel of the crucified servant; those who receive it are those to whom the Father has given eyes to see. The sovereignty of God in salvation and in hardening operates through the free choices of human beings without eliminating those choices.

verseByVerse.quote: "He has blinded their eyes and hardened their heart, lest they see with their eyes, and understand with their heart, and turn, and I would heal them." Isaiah said these things because he saw his glory and spoke of him.
verseByVerse.commentary: Isaiah 6:9-10 — the commission scene where Isaiah is told that his preaching will harden — is applied to the Jews' rejection of Jesus. He has blinded their eyes and hardened their heart: the divine hardening is the judicial confirmation of a direction already chosen. God does not harden those who would otherwise have softened; he confirms the hardness of those who have repeatedly refused the light. Isaiah said these things because he saw his glory: the glory Isaiah saw in the temple (Isa. 6:1-4) was the pre-incarnate glory of the Son. The prophets testify about Christ even when they do not know they are doing so.

verseByVerse.quote: Nevertheless, many even of the authorities believed in him, but for fear of the Pharisees they did not confess it, so that they would not be put out of the synagogue; for they loved the glory that comes from man more than the glory that comes from God.
verseByVerse.commentary: Many of the authorities believed but would not confess: the faith that does not produce confession is a faith at risk. They loved the glory that comes from man more than the glory that comes from God — the precise diagnosis Jesus gave in 5:44. Covert discipleship, while not impossible (Joseph of Arimathea will eventually act publicly), is spiritually dangerous: the pressures that prevent confession also prevent growth, and the faith that cannot be named publicly is faith that has not yet been fully tested. Nicodemus comes by night; eventually he stands by the cross. The trajectory of authentic faith is always toward greater openness, not greater concealment.

verseByVerse.quote: And Jesus cried out and said, "Whoever believes in me, believes not in me but in him who sent me. And whoever sees me sees him who sent me."
verseByVerse.commentary: The final public proclamation of Jesus' ministry (before the farewell discourse) is a summary of everything he has been saying: to believe in him is to believe in the Father; to see him is to see the Father. Jesus is not an alternative to the Father but the Father's self-revelation in human form. This is the heart of the incarnation's meaning: the God who could not be seen (1:18) has made himself visible in the Son. Faith in Jesus is not a human projection onto a religious figure but the response to God's own self-giving. The one who receives Jesus receives the Father who sent him.

verseByVerse.quote: "I have come into the world as light, so that whoever believes in me may not remain in darkness. If anyone hears my words and does not keep them, I do not judge him; for I did not come to judge the world but to save the world."
verseByVerse.commentary: I have come as light: the declaration of the Prologue (1:4-5, 9) is now spoken in first person by the Light himself as his public ministry closes. The purpose is salvation, not condemnation: I did not come to judge but to save. This is the first movement of the gospel — the Son came in love, not in judicial wrath. The judgment comes, but it comes as consequence, not as primary purpose. The one who hears and does not keep is not judged by Jesus directly; he is judged by the word itself on the last day. The gospel is simultaneously the most gracious offer and the most solemn warning in human history.

verseByVerse.quote: "The one who rejects me and does not receive my words has a judge; the word that I have spoken will judge him on the last day. For I have not spoken on my own authority, but the Father who sent me has himself given me a commandment — what to say and what to speak."
verseByVerse.commentary: The word that I have spoken will judge him on the last day: the words of Jesus are not merely historical utterances but active agents of eschatological judgment. The Sermon on the Mount, the bread of life discourse, the I AM sayings — all will stand as evidence on the last day. And the authority of these words is the Father's own authority: Jesus has spoken only what the Father commanded. Rejecting Jesus' words is rejecting the Father's words; the final Judge is the same one who offered himself in the Son. Mercy refused becomes the standard of judgment.

verseByVerse.quote: "And I know that his commandment is eternal life. What I say, therefore, I say as the Father has told me."
verseByVerse.commentary: His commandment is eternal life: the Father's instruction to the Son — the mission, the message, the words — has as its content and goal the eternal life of those who receive it. What Jesus says is what the Father says; the word of the Son is the word of the Father. The public ministry closes with this reminder: everything Jesus has said, every sign, every teaching, every confrontation, every promise — all of it is the Father's eternal life reaching toward humanity in the person of the Son. The gospel is not the Son's independent project; it is the eternal purpose of the Trinity expressed in the Son's mission to the world.

13.title: The Foot Washing and the New Commandment

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–20 — The Foot Washing: Love to the End
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: On the night of his arrest, knowing that his hour has come and that he will return to the Father, Jesus takes a towel and basin and washes his disciples' feet — including Judas'. The enacted parable of servanthood precedes the verbal commandment of love. He who is Lord and Teacher makes himself the servant of all.
verseByVerse.theology: The foot washing is simultaneously a moral example (do as I have done) and a sacramental cleansing (you need to have your feet washed to have a part in me). Peter's characteristic resistance — then misunderstanding, then over-correction — clarifies both aspects: the washing Jesus gives is not merely a lesson in humility but the cleansing that makes fellowship with him possible. The once-washed disciple needs only the cleaning of feet — the ongoing renewal of those already justified, not re-justification. This is the distinction between initial cleansing (bath) and ongoing renewal (feet-washing): the one already clean needs only this.
verseByVerse.examples: You call me Teacher and Lord, and you are right, for so I am (v. 13). The authority of the foot-washing is its own argument. Jesus does not wash feet because he has forgotten who he is; he washes feet because he knows exactly who he is (v. 3-4). The servant heart flows from the secure identity: those who are anxious about their position never serve freely; those who know their position in Christ serve without self-protection. Genuine servanthood is not self-abasement but the overflow of a heart that has been secured by the Father's love.

verseByVerse.quote: Now before the Feast of the Passover, when Jesus knew that his hour had come to depart out of this world to the Father, having loved his own who were in the world, he loved them to the end. During supper, when the devil had already put it into the heart of Judas Iscariot, Simon's son, to betray him,
verseByVerse.commentary: He loved them to the end: the Greek eis telos can mean 'to the end' (of his life) and 'to the uttermost' (completeness of love). Both are true: the cross is the temporal end of his earthly life and the absolute limit of love's self-giving.
