The Passover Feast: the lamb is about to be slaughtered; the true Passover Lamb is hosting his final meal. And already Judas has received the devil's suggestion — the darkness at the table, the night in the disciple's heart. Jesus knows it all and washes Judas' feet anyway. This is love to the end: unwavering even toward the betrayer.

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus, knowing that the Father had given all things into his hands, and that he had come from God and was going to God, rose from supper. He laid aside his outer garments, and taking a towel, tied it around himself.
verseByVerse.commentary: Knowing that the Father had given all things into his hands: the sequence is crucial — because Jesus knows his authority and security, he can serve without self-protection. The servant heart flows from the secure identity; those who are uncertain of their status cannot truly serve because service threatens what they are still trying to establish. He rises, lays aside his outer garment, ties a towel — each action a voluntary divesting of dignity, anticipating the stripping that will occur at Calvary. The incarnation is itself the ultimate laying aside: the eternal Word divesting himself of divine prerogatives to take the form of a servant (Phil. 2:7).

verseByVerse.quote: Then he poured water into a basin and began to wash the disciples' feet and to wipe them with the towel that was wrapped around him. He came to Simon Peter, who said to him, "Lord, do you wash my feet?"
verseByVerse.commentary: Lord, do you wash my feet? — the question is theologically accurate: this is Lord, and it is inconceivable that Lord should wash feet. Peter's objection is not false modesty but genuine christological instinct: something is wrong with this picture. And he is right — except that the wrongness of the picture is precisely the point. The one who should be served serves. The one whose feet should be washed washes. The incarnation and atonement are both versions of the same reversal: the greatest becomes the least, the Lord becomes the servant, the one who deserves worship gives himself as ransom.

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus answered him, "What I am doing you do not know now, but afterward you will understand." Peter said to him, "You shall never wash my feet." Jesus answered him, "If I do not wash you, you have no share with me."
verseByVerse.commentary: If I do not wash you, you have no share with me: the washing is not merely ceremonial humility but the condition of fellowship. Peter's refusal, however pious-sounding, is a refusal of the grace that makes union with Christ possible. The foot-washing is a parable of the atonement: only what Jesus does — the unilateral cleansing from sin's defilement — creates the possibility of abiding with him. You cannot participate in Christ while refusing what he gives. The pattern holds across every form of false humility that refuses grace: 'I'm not worthy' can be a deeper refusal than 'I don't need it.'

verseByVerse.quote: Simon Peter said to him, "Lord, not my feet only but also my hands and my head!" Jesus said to him, "The one who has bathed does not need to wash, except for his feet, but is completely clean. And you are clean, but not all of you."
verseByVerse.commentary: Peter overcorrects: if some is good, more must be better. Jesus' answer distinguishes between the bath (initial justification, complete cleansing from sin's guilt) and the foot-washing (ongoing sanctification, the daily renewal needed as the justified walk through a world that soils the feet). The one already bathed does not need re-justification; he needs daily cleansing from the accumulated defilement of walking in a fallen world. You are clean, but not all of you: Judas is at the table, washed like the rest, but not truly cleansed — because the external washing has not been met with internal reception.

verseByVerse.quote: For he knew who was to betray him; that was why he said, "Not all of you are clean." When he had washed their feet and put on his outer garments and resumed his place, he said to them, "Do you understand what I have done to you?"
verseByVerse.commentary: He knew who was to betray him: Judas has received the foot-washing along with the eleven, but without the transformation it signifies. External participation in the means of grace — baptism, the Lord's Supper, the ministry of the word — does not automatically produce internal cleansing. This is the warning of the sacraments: they are genuine means of grace but not automatically effective apart from faith. When he had resumed his place, he asks the interpretive question: Do you understand what I have done? The teaching always follows the enacted parable; the Spirit always interprets the sign.

verseByVerse.quote: "You call me Teacher and Lord, and you are right, for so I am. If I then, your Lord and Teacher, have washed your feet, you also ought to wash one another's feet."
verseByVerse.commentary: You are right, for so I am: Jesus does not modestly disclaim the titles Teacher and Lord; he affirms them. His servanthood does not diminish his authority; it expresses it in its highest form. Because I am Lord and Teacher and have washed your feet — the argument is from the greater to the lesser. If the one of greater dignity serves those of lesser dignity, how much more should the disciples serve one another? The foot-washing is both example and obligation: the way Jesus loves is the way his people are to love, characterized by the voluntary downward movement of serving those who cannot repay.

verseByVerse.quote: "For I have given you an example, that you also should do just as I have done to you. Truly, truly, I say to you, a servant is not greater than his master, nor is a messenger greater than the one who sent him."
verseByVerse.commentary: I have given you an example: the Greek word hupodeigma means a pattern or model to follow. The foot-washing is not a unique non-repeatable sacrament but a pattern of loving servanthood to be embodied in the community of disciples. A servant is not greater than his master: if the Master washes feet, the servants cannot consider themselves above it. The hierarchy of dignity that the world constructs is consistently inverted in the kingdom: the greatest serves, the first becomes last, the Lord takes the towel. This is not merely counter-cultural; it is counter-natural, requiring the Spirit's work in the community.

verseByVerse.quote: "If you know these things, blessed are you if you do them. I am not speaking of all of you; I know whom I have chosen. But the Scripture will be fulfilled, 'He who ate my bread has lifted his heel against me.'"
verseByVerse.commentary: Blessed are you if you do them: the beatitude of enacted knowledge. It is not enough to understand the principle of servanthood; the blessing comes with the practice. I know whom I have chosen: the election of the twelve included Judas — not in ignorance but in sovereign purpose, so that the Scripture might be fulfilled. He who ate my bread: Psalm 41:9, the betrayal of a trusted companion, now fulfilled in the one who just received the foot-washing. The chosen betrayer and the Scripture's fulfillment are not in tension: God's sovereignty encompasses even the sin that will accomplish his purpose.

verseByVerse.quote: "I am telling you this now, before it takes place, that when it does take place you may believe that I am he. Truly, truly, I say to you, whoever receives the one I send receives me, and whoever receives me receives the one who sent me."
verseByVerse.commentary: I am telling you before it takes place: predictive prophecy in service of faith. When the betrayal happens, the disciples will not conclude that Jesus was surprised or defeated; they will remember that he announced it beforehand and believe more deeply. This is the function of prophecy in John's gospel: not to satisfy curiosity about the future but to produce faith in the past. And the apostolic commission: whoever receives my apostle receives me. The missionary church carries the delegated authority of the one who sent it — to receive the gospel messenger is to receive the gospel Lord.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 21–38 — The Betrayer Exposed and the New Commandment
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Jesus announces that one of the twelve will betray him; the beloved disciple asks who; Jesus identifies Judas with a morsel of bread, who immediately goes out — and it is night. Jesus then announces the new commandment: love one another as I have loved you. Peter's confident declaration of loyalty is met with the prediction of triple denial.
verseByVerse.theology: Love one another as I have loved you is the social ethics of the atonement made into community commandment. The 'as I have loved you' is the measure and the model: not abstract love or sentiment, but the costly, self-giving, foot-washing, cross-bearing love that Jesus has just demonstrated and is about to complete. This is a new commandment not because love was absent from the Mosaic law (Lev. 19:18) but because the standard is new: as I have loved you is qualitatively greater than 'as yourself.' The measure of Christian community love is the cross.
verseByVerse.examples: The prediction of Peter's denial is embedded within Peter's most confident declaration. He will not only follow Jesus but lay down his life for him. Jesus accepts neither the protest nor the probability: Will you lay down your life for me? Truly, truly, I say to you — the triple denial will come before morning. Jesus does not shame Peter but tells the truth that Peter needs to hear: his fidelity rests on a foundation Peter has not yet tested. The testing will come, the failure will happen, and the restoration that follows (ch. 21) will be built on a more honest foundation than confidence ever was.

verseByVerse.quote: After saying these things, Jesus was troubled in his spirit, and testified, "Truly, truly, I say to you, one of you will betray me." The disciples looked at one another, uncertain of whom he spoke.
verseByVerse.commentary: Jesus was troubled in his spirit: the same word as at the tomb of Lazarus — genuine inner disturbance at the proximity of evil and death. The announcement — one of you — is devastating in its application. One of the twelve: the betrayer is not a stranger but a companion of the table. Uncertain of whom he spoke: the disciples cannot identify the traitor, which is itself a comment on the subtlety of Judas' performance. He has been indistinguishable from the rest in his outward discipleship. The traitor in the community is never obviously different until the betrayal occurs.

verseByVerse.quote: One of his disciples, whom Jesus loved, was reclining at table at Jesus' side — Simon Peter therefore motioned to him to ask Jesus of whom he was speaking.
verseByVerse.commentary: The beloved disciple — John, typically understood — reclines closest to Jesus at the Passover posture, at his side. Peter, always the spokesman, uses his proximity through the beloved disciple: find out. The beloved disciple's position is both physical (next to Jesus) and relational (the model of the disciple who receives and believes). Peter, who will soon fail most visibly, organizes the inquiry; John, who will stand at the cross, is already in the place of intimate witness. Their roles at this supper anticipate their roles in the passion narrative.

verseByVerse.quote: So that disciple, leaning back against Jesus, asked him, "Lord, who is it?" Jesus answered, "It is he to whom I will give this morsel of bread when I have dipped it." So when he had dipped the morsel, he gave it to Judas, the son of Simon Iscariot.
verseByVerse.commentary: The dipped morsel given to Judas is a gesture of honor — the host giving a choice piece to a guest — and simultaneously the identification of the betrayer. Jesus honors the one who will betray him with the gesture of distinction. Love to the end means that even the identification of the traitor is performed through an act of love, not contempt. Judas receives the morsel that names him and seals him; the sacramental gesture (bread given, bread received) is a bitter parody of what it could have been. Grace offered and refused becomes the occasion of judgment.

verseByVerse.quote: Then after he had taken the morsel, Satan entered into him. Jesus said to him, "What you are going to do, do quickly." Now no one at the table knew why he said this to him.
verseByVerse.commentary: Satan entered into him: the morsel accepted without faith becomes the moment of full satanic possession. Judas has been incrementally moving toward this since the complaint about the ointment (12:6); now the movement is complete. Jesus' command — do quickly — is not surrender but sovereignty: Jesus is not reacting to Judas's plan but directing its timing. The betrayal will happen on Jesus' schedule, not Judas's. The disciples' incomprehension (no one knew why) is part of the pattern: the cross is not understood until the Spirit interprets it through the lens of resurrection.

verseByVerse.quote: Some thought that, because Judas had the moneybag, Jesus was telling him, "Buy what we need for the feast," or that he should give something to the poor. So, after receiving the morsel of bread, he immediately went out. And it was night.
verseByVerse.commentary: And it was night: three of the most ominous words in John's gospel. Judas walks out of the light into the darkness — literally (it is after sunset) and spiritually (he has left the presence of the Light of the world). The disciples' misreading — perhaps he's gone to buy food or give to the poor — is characteristic. The forces of darkness always have their cover story; the traitor always has a plausible explanation. Night falls when the betrayer exits; the darkness that John has been using as theological symbol throughout the gospel is now literal and personal. The ruler of darkness is about to have his hour.

verseByVerse.quote: When he had gone out, Jesus said, "Now is the Son of Man glorified, and God is glorified in him. If God is glorified in him, God will also glorify him in himself, and glorify him at once."
verseByVerse.commentary: Now is the Son of Man glorified: the departure of Judas into the night is the beginning of the passion sequence, and Jesus greets it as the moment of glorification. The cross is glory — not despite its suffering but through it. The mutual glorification of Father and Son in the passion: the Son glorifies the Father by perfect obedience to the saving will; the Father glorifies the Son by resurrection and exaltation. And glorify him at once: not after a long delay but immediately — the resurrection is three days away. The certainty of the vindication is already present in the announcement.

verseByVerse.quote: "Little children, yet a little while I am with you. You will seek me, and just as I said to the Jews, so now I say to you, 'Where I am going you cannot come.' A new commandment I give to you, that you love one another: just as I have loved you, you also are to love one another."
verseByVerse.commentary: Little children: the term of deep paternal affection, used only here in the gospel (though characteristic of 1 John). The farewell is coming. And then immediately: the new commandment. Love one another: not new in content (Lev. 19:18) but new in standard. As I have loved you — the foot-washing, the cross, the self-giving unto death — this is now the measure. The community of the Crucified One is called to embody cruciform love in its own common life. The new covenant community is defined not by ethnic identity or ritual observance but by the quality of love that mirrors the love of its Lord.

verseByVerse.quote: "By this all people will know that you are my disciples, if you have love for one another." Simon Peter said to him, "Lord, where are you going?" Jesus answered him, "Where I am going you cannot follow me now, but you will follow afterward."
verseByVerse.commentary: By this all people will know: the public witness of the church is its love. Not its doctrine alone, not its correct theology, not its moral achievement — the love that mirrors the cross is the testimony that cannot be fabricated. The world can argue with theology; it has no argument against a community that genuinely loves the unlovable, forgives the unforgivable, serves the unworthy. You will follow afterward: Peter will eventually follow Jesus into death — tradition records his crucifixion in Rome. The 'not now' is not permanent exclusion but postponement; the cross that separates them now will be the path Peter himself eventually walks.

verseByVerse.quote: Peter said to him, "Lord, why can I not follow you now? I will lay down my life for you." Jesus answered, "Will you lay down your life for me? Truly, truly, I say to you, the rooster will not crow till you have denied me three times."
verseByVerse.commentary: I will lay down my life for you: the same language Jesus used for the good shepherd (10:11, 15). Peter means it; he is not insincere. But he does not yet know himself. Jesus' prediction — the rooster, the three denials, before morning — is spoken not to shame Peter but to prepare him. When the denial comes, Peter will remember these words (Luke 22:61) and weep bitterly — the beginning of the restoration that will be completed in chapter 21. The prediction of failure is an act of mercy: it ensures that when the failure happens, Peter interprets it through what Jesus said, not through despair.

14.title: I Am the Way, the Truth, and the Life

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–14 — The Way to the Father
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Jesus comforts the disciples with the promise of prepared dwelling places in the Father's house, declares himself the way, the truth, and the life, and responds to Philip's request to see the Father with the most concentrated statement of his unity with the Father in the farewell discourse. Prayer in his name is grounded in this unity.
verseByVerse.theology: I am the way, the truth, and the life; no one comes to the Father except through me is both comfort and exclusivity. Comfort: there is a way to the Father, it is real, it is accessible, it is Jesus. Exclusivity: this is the only way, and all other paths are paths that do not lead to the Father. The exclusivity is not arrogance; it is the necessary consequence of the incarnation. If God has come in one place, in one person, for one purpose, then there is one way home. The scandal of particularity cannot be removed without removing the gospel itself.
verseByVerse.examples: Whatever you ask in my name, this I will do (v. 13). Prayer in Jesus' name is not a formula attached to the end of requests; it is prayer aligned with his character, his purposes, and his glory. To ask in Jesus' name is to ask as he would ask, for what he would ask for, in the way that honors the Father through the Son. This is why prayer in Jesus' name is effective: it brings human desire into alignment with divine will, and divine will always accomplishes its purpose.

verseByVerse.quote: "Let not your hearts be troubled. Believe in God; believe also in me. In my Father's house are many rooms. If it were not so, would I have told you that I go to prepare a place for you?"
verseByVerse.commentary: Let not your hearts be troubled: the command does not deny the trouble but addresses it with a double call to faith — believe in God, believe also in me. The foundation of untroubled hearts is not the absence of difficulty but the presence of the one who has said these words. In my Father's house are many rooms: the Greek monai (rooms, dwellings) suggests permanent, settled habitation — not temporary lodging but the permanent dwelling of the Father's household. The many rooms accommodate the diversity of those who will come; there is room for all the Father has given the Son. I go to prepare a place: the cross is the preparation, the resurrection is the completion.

verseByVerse.quote: "And if I go and prepare a place for you, I will come again and will take you to myself, that where I am you may be also. And you know the way to where I am going."
verseByVerse.commentary: I will come again: the parousia, the return of Christ, promised in the farewell discourse. The purpose of the return is personal — not merely to judge the world but to take his people to himself: that where I am you may be also. Union with Christ is the substance of eternal life; wherever Christ is, that is where the Christian belongs. You know the way: the disciples do not yet know they know it, as Thomas's question immediately reveals. The way is Jesus himself — they have been walking it for three years without naming it. The familiar is often the last thing to be recognized.

verseByVerse.quote: Thomas said to him, "Lord, we do not know where you are going. How can we know the way?" Jesus said to him, "I am the way, and the truth, and the life. No one comes to the Father except through me."
verseByVerse.commentary: I am the way, the truth, and the life: the sixth great I AM saying of the gospel, and the most comprehensive. Way: the path, the road, the direction — Jesus is not merely the guide to the destination but the path itself. Truth: not merely accurate information but the reality that corresponds to ultimate existence — God as he is. Life: not biological existence but the life of God shared with humanity, the eternal life that begins now and continues forever. No one comes to the Father except through me: the most exclusive claim in human history, spoken by the one whose resurrection vindicates it.

verseByVerse.quote: "If you had known me, you would have known my Father also. From now on you do know him and have seen him." Philip said to him, "Lord, show us the Father, and it is enough for us."
verseByVerse.commentary: From now on you do know him and have seen him: the disciples have been in the presence of the Father's self-disclosure for three years without fully grasping it. From now on — from this moment of declaration — they can understand that every encounter with Jesus has been an encounter with the Father. Philip's request — show us the Father — is the deepest human longing expressed in the most direct possible way. It is also the request that has already been answered. Like the disciples in the boat asking if Jesus is a ghost (Matt. 14:26), they are asking for what has been present all along.

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus said to him, "Have I been with you so long, and you still do not know me, Philip? Whoever has seen me has seen the Father. How can you say, 'Show us the Father'? Do you not believe that I am in the Father and the Father is in me? The words that I say to you I do not speak on my own authority, but the Father who dwells in me does his works."
verseByVerse.commentary: Whoever has seen me has seen the Father: the most direct identification of Jesus with the Father in the entire gospel. The mutual indwelling — I am in the Father and the Father is in me — is the metaphysical ground of the moral claim: what Jesus says is what the Father says, what Jesus does is what the Father does. The Father who dwells in me does his works: the miracles are not Jesus' independent demonstrations but the Father's acts performed through the Son's incarnate presence. The unity of the Trinity is expressed in the unity of words and works.

verseByVerse.quote: "Believe me that I am in the Father and the Father is in me, or else believe on account of the works themselves. Truly, truly, I say to you, whoever believes in me will also do the works that I do; and greater works than these will he do, because I am going to the Father."
verseByVerse.commentary: Greater works than these will he do: not greater in miraculous power (no one heals the blind and raises the dead more dramatically than Jesus) but greater in scope — the apostolic mission will encompass the world, bearing the gospel of the crucified and risen Lord through the Spirit's power. The greater works are the harvest of Pentecost: three thousand in a day, the Gentile mission, the planting of churches across the Mediterranean world. Because I am going to the Father: the ascension releases the Spirit, who empowers the greater works. The departure of the Son is the precondition of the greater ministry of the Spirit.

verseByVerse.quote: "Whatever you ask in my name, this I will do, that the Father may be glorified in the Son. If you ask me anything in my name, I will do it."
verseByVerse.commentary: Whatever you ask in my name: the promise is anchored in the purpose — that the Father may be glorified in the Son. Prayer in Jesus' name is not a formula but an alignment: asking as Jesus would ask, for what Jesus would ask for, in the confidence that the Son's relationship with the Father guarantees the answer. This is not a blank check for self-interested prayer but an invitation into the Son's own posture before the Father — always seeking the Father's glory, always aligned with the Father's will. The promise is real precisely because it is bounded by the name that carries the character of the one who always did what pleased the Father.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 15–31 — The Promise of the Spirit and the Peace of Christ
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Jesus promises another Helper — the Spirit of truth — who will abide with the disciples forever, teaching them all things and bringing to remembrance all that Jesus has said. He gives his peace and prepares them for his departure, explaining that his going to the Father is for their benefit and that his obedience to the Father's command is itself the world's instruction.
verseByVerse.theology: The Helper (Parakletos — Advocate, Comforter, Counselor) is described with four characteristics in the farewell discourse: he is the Spirit of truth (14:17), the Holy Spirit who teaches and reminds (14:26), the Spirit who testifies about Jesus (15:26), and the one who convicts the world (16:8). Each characteristic is an aspect of the single mission: to continue and apply what Jesus accomplished. The Spirit does not bring new revelation beyond Jesus but illuminates everything Jesus said and did, making it present and personal to each generation of believers.
verseByVerse.examples: My peace I give to you: not as the world gives. The world's peace is the absence of conflict, the management of anxiety, the temporary resolution of problems. Jesus' peace is an interior stability that coexists with external trouble — the shalom of the covenant, the wholeness that comes from being right with God and secure in his love. Not as the world gives: the two kinds of peace are not on the same spectrum; one is the presence of order, the other is the presence of God. The disciples will need this peace before the night is over.

verseByVerse.quote: "If you love me, you will keep my commandments. And I will ask the Father, and he will give you another Helper, to be with you forever,"
verseByVerse.commentary: If you love me, you will keep my commandments: not 'keep my commandments and I will believe you love me' but the natural outflow of love producing obedience. Obedience is not the condition of Jesus' love but the evidence of the disciples'. Love and obedience are inseparable in the new covenant: the Spirit who is given writes the law on the heart, creating the desire to obey that the law alone could not create. Another Helper: the Greek allon (another of the same kind) — another Paraclete, because Jesus himself has been the first (1 John 2:1). The Spirit continues the ministry of the one who is departing.

verseByVerse.quote: "even the Spirit of truth, whom the world cannot receive, because it neither sees him nor knows him. You know him, for he dwells with you and will be in you. I will not leave you as orphans; I will come to you."
verseByVerse.commentary: The world cannot receive the Spirit of truth: the natural mind is incapable of recognizing the Spirit because the Spirit's presence requires the new birth that creates spiritual perception. The disciples know him because he has been at work in them through Jesus' ministry; after Pentecost, the Spirit will be in them — a distinction between the external work of the Spirit (with you) and the indwelling gift of the Spirit (in you) that marks the new covenant age. I will not leave you as orphans: the fatherly concern behind the entire farewell discourse — Jesus is preparing, not abandoning, his disciples.

verseByVerse.quote: "Yet a little while and the world will see me no more, but you will see me. Because I live, you also will live. In that day you will know that I am in my Father, and you in me, and I in you."
verseByVerse.commentary: Because I live, you also will live: the resurrection of Jesus is the ground of the disciples' life — both spiritually (they are alive in him) and eschatologically (they will be raised as he was raised). In that day — the day of resurrection, the day of Pentecost, the day of the Spirit's illumination — they will know the mutual indwelling: Jesus in the Father, they in Jesus, Jesus in them. The union of the Trinity becomes the template for the union of Christ and his people: the perichoresis of Father, Son, and Spirit has its analogical echo in the indwelling of Christ and the believer through the Spirit.

verseByVerse.quote: "Whoever has my commandments and keeps them, he it is who loves me. And he who loves me will be loved by my Father, and I will love him and manifest myself to him." Judas (not Iscariot) said to him, "Lord, how is it that you will manifest yourself to us, and not to the world?"
verseByVerse.commentary: Whoever has my commandments and keeps them — loves me: the third iteration of the love-obedience correlation. The repeated emphasis signals its importance: love for Christ is not sentiment but allegiance expressed in the pattern of life. And he who loves me will be loved by my Father: the chain of love — Father loving the Son, the Son loving the disciple who loves the Son, the Father loving the disciple — is the inner logic of the new covenant. Judas (not Iscariot)'s question is genuinely perplexed: how can Jesus manifest himself to some and not to all? The answer will be the Spirit's distinctive work in the community of faith.

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus answered him, "If anyone loves me, he will keep my word, and my Father will love him, and we will come to him and make our home with him. Whoever does not love me does not keep my words. And the word that you hear is not mine but the Father's who sent me."
verseByVerse.commentary: We will come to him and make our home with him: the Trinitarian indwelling in the believer — both Father and Son making their dwelling in the one who loves and obeys. This is the fulfillment of the temple promise: God dwelling with his people, not in a building of stone but in the human spirit renewed by the Holy Spirit. The word heard is the Father's — ultimate authority, divine origin. Those who reject Jesus' words reject not merely a teacher's instruction but the Father's own word to the world. The stakes of hearing the gospel are as high as the source of the gospel is high.

verseByVerse.quote: "These things I have spoken to you while I am still with you. But the Helper, the Holy Spirit, whom the Father will send in my name, he will teach you all things and bring to your remembrance all that I have said to you."
verseByVerse.commentary: He will teach you all things and bring to your remembrance all that I have said: the promise that grounds the authority of the apostolic witness. The disciples could not understand everything Jesus said during his ministry; the Spirit's post-resurrection illumination brought those words to life with new comprehension. This is the inspiration of the New Testament: not dictation of new information but the Spirit's illumination of what Jesus said and did, producing the apostolic witness that became Scripture. The Spirit who reminds is the Spirit who guarantees the reliability of the gospel record.

verseByVerse.quote: "Peace I leave with you; my peace I give to you. Not as the world gives do I give to you. Let not your hearts be troubled, neither let them be afraid. You heard me say to you, 'I am going away, and I will come to you.' If you loved me, you would have rejoiced, because I am going to the Father, for the Father is greater than I."
verseByVerse.commentary: My peace I give to you: the covenant shalom, the wholeness of right relationship with God, given as a bequest from the one who purchased it at the cross. Not as the world gives: the world's peace is temporary, conditional, and dependent on circumstances; Christ's peace is rooted in what he has accomplished and cannot be taken by any external event. The Father is greater than I: within the economy of the incarnation, the Son who has taken the form of a servant operates in dependence on the Father. This is not a statement of ontological subordination (the Son is less than God) but of economic subordination in the mission of redemption.

verseByVerse.quote: "And now I have told you before it takes place, so that when it does take place you may believe. I will no longer talk much with you, for the ruler of this world is coming. He has no claim on me,"
verseByVerse.commentary: I have told you before it takes place: the same purpose as 13:19 — predictive announcement in service of post-event faith. The disciples will endure the passion with greater faith because they remember these words. The ruler of this world is coming: the devil approaches through Judas, the soldiers, the arrest — and yet he has no claim on Jesus. The Greek has no power over me or no claim on me: the sinless Son is not subject to the devil's leverage. Sin gives the enemy his foothold; where there is no sin, there is no purchase. Jesus goes to the cross not because the enemy captures him but because the Father's love calls him.

verseByVerse.quote: "but I do as the Father has commanded me, so that the world may know that I love the Father. Rise, let us go from here."
verseByVerse.commentary: I do as the Father has commanded me: the voluntary obedience of the Son is the world's instruction in what love for the Father looks like. The cross is not merely substitutionary atonement (though it is certainly that); it is also the supreme display of filial love — the Son doing what the Father commands because he loves the Father, giving the world a visible image of the inner-Trinitarian love that is the foundation of all reality. Rise, let us go from here: the departure from the upper room into Gethsemane, into the night where the ruler of the world waits. The Son goes forward in love, not in coercion. Let us go.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–17 — Abide in Me: The Vine and the Branches
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Jesus declares himself the true vine and the Father the vinedresser, then calls his disciples to abide in him as branches abide in the vine — the condition of fruitfulness. Pruning, abiding, and bearing fruit are the central images. The section closes with the commandment to love one another as Jesus has loved, grounded in the friendship that replaces servant-status.
verseByVerse.theology: I am the true vine: Israel was the vine God planted (Ps. 80:8; Isa. 5:1-7; Jer. 2:21; Ezek. 15; Hos. 10:1). Israel repeatedly failed as the vine. Jesus is the vine Israel was always meant to be — the true Israel, the faithful son, the one who bears fruit that lasts. The disciples are branches in this vine: their fruitfulness is entirely dependent on their connection to Jesus. Apart from me you can do nothing is the Reformed doctrine of total human dependence stated for the community of disciples. The branch does not produce fruit; it bears fruit — the distinction between human effort and Spirit-mediated connection.
verseByVerse.examples: You did not choose me, but I chose you (v. 16): the elective basis of discipleship. The disciples' following of Jesus is traced back to his choosing, not their decision. This does not make the disciples passive; they are appointed to go and bear fruit. But the initiative, the foundation, and the guarantee of fruitfulness reside in the one who chose, not in those who were chosen. Whatever fruit the Christian life produces is the fruit of the Vine, borne through the branches who abide.

verseByVerse.quote: "I am the true vine, and my Father is the vinedresser. Every branch in me that does not bear fruit he takes away, and every branch that does bear fruit he prunes, that it may bear more fruit."
verseByVerse.commentary: I am the true vine: the seventh and final great I AM saying of the gospel. Israel was God's vine (Ps. 80:8; Isa. 5:1-7), repeatedly failing, repeatedly cut back. Jesus is the true vine — the faithful Israel, the son who does what the national son could not do. The Father as vinedresser: the pruning is not punishment but cultivation — the same care applied to the fruitful branch as to the unfruitful, though differently. The fruitful branch is pruned so that it might bear more fruit. Sanctification understood as divine pruning: God cuts away what is good to produce what is better, removes what is comfortable to make room for what is fruitful.

verseByVerse.quote: "Already you are clean because of the word that I have spoken to you. Abide in me, and I in you. As the branch cannot bear fruit by itself, unless it abides in the vine, neither can you, unless you abide in me."
verseByVerse.commentary: Already you are clean: the cleansing of the disciples has already taken place through the word — the teaching that has been received and has done its purifying work. The foot-washing (13:10) and the word have accomplished the initial cleansing; now the ongoing condition is abiding. Abide in me, and I in you: the mutual indwelling is the condition of fruitfulness. The branch that is cut off — whatever its appearance or past — cannot bear fruit apart from the vine. This is the dependence that pride always resists and grace always establishes: apart from me you can do nothing, which means with me, everything.

verseByVerse.quote: "I am the vine; you are the branches. Whoever abides in me and I in him, he it is that bears much fruit, for apart from me you can do nothing. If anyone does not abide in me he is thrown away like a branch and withers; and the branches are gathered, thrown into the fire, and burned."
verseByVerse.commentary: Apart from me you can do nothing: the most absolute statement of dependence in the gospel. Not a little, not very much — nothing. The branch that is separated from the vine does not produce diminished fruit; it produces no fruit at all. This is the radical impossibility of autonomous Christian living: spiritual fruitfulness requires constant connection, not occasional contact. The warning is equally stark: the non-abiding branch is thrown away and burned. This is not casual; it is the description of apostasy — the branch that seemed to be in the vine but had no living connection is finally revealed and removed.

verseByVerse.quote: "If you abide in me, and my words abide in you, ask whatever you wish, and it will be done for you. By this my Father is glorified, that you bear much fruit and so prove to be my disciples."
verseByVerse.commentary: If you abide in me and my words abide in you: the two-directional abiding — in the person of Christ and in the word of Christ. The word abiding in the disciple creates the desires that prayer then expresses; prayers formed by the word of Christ are prayers aligned with the will of Christ, which the Father always answers. By this my Father is glorified: the glory of God and the fruitfulness of the disciples are inseparably connected. The church's mission to bear much fruit is not self-aggrandizement but Father-glorification. The Vine's purpose is the vinedresser's glory; the branches exist to honor the one who plants and tends.

verseByVerse.quote: "As the Father has loved me, so have I loved you. Abide in my love. If you keep my commandments, you will abide in my love, just as I have kept my Father's commandments and abide in his love."
verseByVerse.commentary: As the Father has loved me, so have I loved you: the love of the disciples is patterned on and derived from the inner-Trinitarian love of Father and Son. The disciples are loved with the same quality of love that flows eternally between the Father and Son. Abide in my love: love is not merely a feeling to be received but a sphere to live within. Keeping my commandments is not the condition of earning love but the way of remaining in the love already given — as Jesus' own obedience to the Father's commandments is the expression of his abiding in the Father's love. Obedience is love's response, not love's price.

verseByVerse.quote: "These things I have spoken to you, that my joy may be in you, and that your joy may be full. This is my commandment, that you love one another as I have loved you."
verseByVerse.commentary: That my joy may be in you: the purpose of the entire farewell discourse is not merely to prepare the disciples for suffering but to fill them with the joy that belongs to Jesus himself — the joy that exists in the inner-Trinitarian fellowship of perfect love and perfect obedience. Full joy is the overflow of abiding in the vine. And then the commandment: love one another as I have loved you. The vine and the branches metaphor now becomes the basis for community ethics: branches in the same vine are branches in relationship with each other. The love of Christ for the disciples becomes the measure of their love for one another.

verseByVerse.quote: "Greater love has no one than this, that someone lay down his life for his friends. You are my friends if you do what I command you."
verseByVerse.commentary: Greater love has no one than this: the cross stated as the universal criterion of love's greatness. Not romantic love, not familial love, but the love that gives itself for the beloved at the cost of life itself — this is the greatest love. The disciples are not merely servants now but friends — those admitted to the confidence of the one who chose them (v. 15). The friendship is conditional not because it must be earned but because it is accepted by those who respond to what Jesus commands. Command and friendship coexist: the one who commands is the friend who has laid down his life for those he commands.

verseByVerse.quote: "No longer do I call you servants, for the servant does not know what his master is doing; but I have called you friends, for all that I have heard from my Father I have made known to you. You did not choose me, but I chose you and appointed you that you should go and bear fruit and that your fruit should abide, so that whatever you ask the Father in my name, he may give it to you."
verseByVerse.commentary: You did not choose me, but I chose you: the elective foundation of discipleship. The disciples' following of Jesus traces not to their initiative but to his choosing. This is not the language of passive automatons but of those whose freedom has been liberated and directed by grace. Appointed to go and bear fruit that abides: the election is unto mission, fruitfulness, and the prayer-connection that sustains both. The same prayer promise (ask in my name) that appears in 14:13-14 reappears here, anchored now in election — those whom God chose are the ones whose prayers in Jesus' name the Father answers.

verseByVerse.quote: "These things I command you, so that you will love one another."
verseByVerse.commentary: The entire farewell discourse, the vine-and-branches discourse, the election and appointment — all of it is commanded so that you will love one another. The theological richness of chapters 13-17 is not an end in itself; it is the foundation for community love. Reformed theology at its best is always this: the doctrine of election produces humility; the doctrine of grace produces gratitude; both produce the servant-hearted love of the community of the chosen. The commandment to love is not imposed on top of the theology but is the practical expression of everything the theology has established.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 18–27 — The World's Hatred and the Spirit's Witness
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Jesus prepares the disciples for the world's hatred: as the world hated him, it will hate them. The hatred is not arbitrary but the inevitable response of darkness to light. Jesus traces the hatred to his own relationship with the Father and promises the Spirit of truth who will bear witness about him — alongside the disciples' own witness.
verseByVerse.theology: The world's hatred of the church is not an accident to be explained away but a structural feature of the relationship between the kingdom of God and the kingdom of this world. Jesus does not promise that clever strategy or cultural accommodation will eliminate the hatred; he promises that the Spirit will sustain the witnesses through it. The Spirit of truth who proceeds from the Father (v. 26) — a phrase that has generated centuries of debate about the procession of the Spirit — testifies about Jesus, and the disciples testify because they have been with Jesus from the beginning.
verseByVerse.examples: If they persecuted me, they will also persecute you (v. 20). The disciple is not above the master. This is simultaneously warning and honor: to be persecuted for Christ is to share in Christ's experience, to enter the fellowship of his sufferings. The church that is never persecuted has either been culturally absorbed to the point of invisibility or is living in an extraordinarily tolerant society — possibly both. The cross-bearing disciple should expect the world's hostility as confirmation, not contradiction, of authentic discipleship.

verseByVerse.quote: "If the world hates you, know that it has hated me before it hated you. If you were of the world, the world would love you as its own; but because you are not of the world, but I chose you out of the world, therefore the world hates you."
verseByVerse.commentary: Know that it has hated me before it hated you: the disciples' persecution is not unique but participatory — they share in Jesus' experience because they share his identity. If you were of the world: the world loves its own, a statement of the social logic of the fallen order. The disciples have been chosen out of the world — extracted from the world's value system, called to different loyalties, marked by a different love. This chosenness is the source of both their dignity and their danger. Election unto discipleship is election unto suffering; there is no way to be chosen by God and remain comfortable in the world that rejected God's Son.

verseByVerse.quote: "Remember the word that I said to you: 'A servant is not greater than his master.' If they persecuted me, they will also persecute you. If they kept my word, they will also keep yours. But all these things they will do to you on account of my name, because they do not know him who sent me."
verseByVerse.commentary: If they persecuted me, they will also persecute you: the logic of identification runs in both directions. The world's treatment of the disciples mirrors its treatment of Jesus because it sees in the disciples the presence of Jesus. On account of my name: persecution of the church is ultimately directed at Christ. The world that does not know the Father does not recognize the Father's messengers; the ignorance is not innocent but culpable — they have had the opportunity to know and refused. This is why persecution is not random but patterned: it concentrates around those who most clearly bear the name and character of Christ.

verseByVerse.quote: "If I had not come and spoken to them, they would not have been guilty of sin, but now they have no excuse for their sin. Whoever hates me hates my Father also."
verseByVerse.commentary: Now they have no excuse: the coming of Jesus and his teaching has removed the plausible excuse of ignorance. Moral and spiritual responsibility is proportional to light received. The Jews who heard Jesus, saw his signs, and rejected him bear a heavier responsibility than those who never had the opportunity. Whoever hates me hates my Father also: the inseparability of Father and Son means that rejection of the Son is rejection of the Father. Those who claim to honor God while opposing Jesus are in self-contradiction; the God they honor has sent the Son they reject.

verseByVerse.quote: "If I had not done among them the works that no one else did, they would not be guilty of sin, but now they have seen and hated both me and my Father. But the word that is written in their Law must be fulfilled: 'They hated me without a cause.'"
verseByVerse.commentary: Works that no one else did: the signs are themselves witness, and rejection of the signs is culpable because the evidence is overwhelming. Psalm 35:19 and 69:4 — they hated me without cause — are applied to the rejection of Jesus. The hatred is causeless in the sense that Jesus gave no legitimate occasion for it: no sin, no deception, no injustice. The hatred is the pure expression of the world's alienation from God, unmasked by the presence of perfect goodness. When perfect love is rejected by the world, the world's enmity against God becomes fully visible. The cross reveals both sides: God's love and the world's hatred of it.

verseByVerse.quote: "But when the Helper comes, whom I will send to you from the Father, the Spirit of truth, who proceeds from the Father, he will bear witness about me. And you also will bear witness, because you have been with me from the beginning."
verseByVerse.commentary: The Spirit of truth who proceeds from the Father: the double mission of the Spirit — from the Father, sent by the Son — is the basis of the great filioque controversy that divided Eastern and Western Christianity. Whatever the precise formulation, the Spirit's testimony is the primary witness about Jesus in the world after the ascension. And the disciples will bear witness because they have been with Jesus from the beginning: the apostolic witness is grounded in eyewitness experience, and the Spirit will illuminate and sustain that witness across generations. The Spirit and the church together continue the testimony to Christ that will not be silenced.

16.title: The Spirit and the Joy of the Disciples

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–15 — The Spirit Convicts the World
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Jesus continues warning the disciples about persecution, explaining that telling them in advance is itself an act of pastoral care. He promises the Spirit who will convict the world concerning sin, righteousness, and judgment, and will guide the disciples into all truth — not independently but in full dependence on what he receives from the Son and Father.
verseByVerse.theology: The conviction work of the Spirit operates on three fronts: sin (the world's refusal to believe in Jesus), righteousness (the vindication of Jesus in his ascension to the Father), and judgment (the condemnation of the ruler of this world at the cross). This Trinitarian work of conviction is not coercive but illuminating — the Spirit opens eyes to what is actually true about the world's condition, about Jesus' identity, and about the decisive verdict already rendered at Calvary. Evangelism that presents the gospel as optional enhancement rather than rescue from genuine condemnation has not yet let the Spirit do his convicting work.
verseByVerse.examples: He will guide you into all truth (v. 13): the Spirit's hermeneutical function is ongoing, not merely the initial inspiration of the apostolic witness. The community that has the Spirit has access to the interpretive presence of the one who knows the mind of God (1 Cor. 2:10-11). This does not mean every Christian's interpretation is equally valid; it means that the Spirit-guided community reading the Spirit-inspired text under the guidance of the Spirit's teaching office can arrive at the truth Jesus promised. The church's theology is a work of the Spirit.

verseByVerse.quote: "I have said all these things to you to keep you from falling away. They will put you out of the synagogues. Indeed, the hour is coming when whoever kills you will think he is offering service to God."
verseByVerse.commentary: To keep you from falling away: the purpose of the persecution warning is not to terrify but to fortify. Forewarned disciples are not surprised disciples; they can interpret their suffering through the framework Jesus has given. Whoever kills you will think he is offering service to God: the most dangerous form of persecution is the kind motivated by religious conviction. The Zealot who kills a Christian for apostasy, the inquisitor who burns the heretic for God's honor, the jihadist who executes the infidel — all believe they serve God. This religious violence is not a contradiction of religion but the expression of religion that has become severed from knowledge of the Father (v. 3).

verseByVerse.quote: "And they will do these things because they have not known the Father, nor me. But I have said these things to you, that when their hour comes you may remember that I told them to you. I did not say these things to you from the beginning, because I was with you."
verseByVerse.commentary: They have not known the Father, nor me: the theological root of religious violence. Those who truly know the Father — who has sent the Son, who loves the world, whose nature is self-giving grace — cannot persist in violence against those who bear the Son's name. Religious persecution is always a form of theological ignorance dressed in piety. I told them to you: the remembered word of Jesus is the anchor for the disciple under pressure. When the persecution comes, the memory of these words produces not despair but confirmatory faith: this is what he said would happen, and it is happening, therefore he is true.

verseByVerse.quote: "But now I am going to him who sent me, and none of you asks me, 'Where are you going?' But because I have said these things to you, sorrow has filled your heart."
verseByVerse.commentary: None of you asks me where I am going: Peter did ask (13:36), and Thomas did ask about the way (14:5), but now in the face of the full disclosure of what lies ahead, the disciples are overwhelmed by sorrow and have stopped asking the theological question. Sorrow has filled your heart: the disciples are in grief, processing the news of Jesus' departure and the coming persecution. Their grief is real and Jesus acknowledges it — he does not minimize it. But what they cannot yet see is that his departure is the precondition of a greater presence, not its termination.

verseByVerse.quote: "Nevertheless, I tell you the truth: it is to your advantage that I go away, for if I do not go away, the Helper will not come to you. But if I go, I will send him to you. And when he comes, he will convict the world concerning sin and righteousness and judgment:"
verseByVerse.commentary: It is to your advantage that I go away: the most counterintuitive statement of the farewell discourse. How can the physical absence of Jesus be better than his physical presence? Because the Spirit, given through the glorification of the Son, creates a presence that is not limited by geography. Jesus in the flesh could only be in one place at a time; the Spirit indwells every believer simultaneously in every location. The church's global expansion required the local limitation of the incarnation to give way to the universal presence of the Spirit. The going away is itself an act of love for the entire world, not only for the disciples in that upper room.

verseByVerse.quote: "concerning sin, because they do not believe in me; concerning righteousness, because I go to the Father, and you will see me no longer;"
verseByVerse.commentary: Concerning sin, because they do not believe in me: the Spirit's conviction of sin does not begin with a catalogue of moral failures but with the root sin — the rejection of the Son. Every other sin is a fruit of this tree. The Spirit's work of evangelism is to expose the fundamental wrong that underlies all wrong: alienation from God expressed as refusal of the one God sent. Concerning righteousness, because I go to the Father: Jesus' ascension is the Father's vindication — he who was condemned by the world as a blasphemer and criminal is welcomed into the Father's glory, demonstrating that he was righteous all along. The Spirit announces that righteousness.

verseByVerse.quote: "concerning judgment, because the ruler of this world is judged. I still have many things to say to you, but you cannot bear them now."
verseByVerse.commentary: Concerning judgment, because the ruler of this world is judged: the cross was the decisive judgment of the devil. The Spirit convicts the world that the verdict of Calvary is permanent and binding — the enemy has been condemned, death has been overcome, the power of accusation has been broken. You cannot bear them now: the pastoral restraint of a teacher who knows what his students can receive. Not all revelation is given at once; the Spirit will guide into truth progressively as the disciples are able to receive it. This is the principle of theological development — not new revelation but the deepening reception of what was always there.

verseByVerse.quote: "When the Spirit of truth comes, he will guide you into all the truth, for he will not speak on his own authority, but whatever he hears he will speak, and he will declare to you the things that are to come. He will glorify me, for he will take what is mine and declare it to you."
verseByVerse.commentary: He will guide you into all the truth: not all truth about everything (chemistry, politics, astronomy) but the truth about God, salvation, and the meaning of Jesus. The Spirit's guidance is not autonomous new revelation but the illumination of what Christ has already accomplished and revealed. He will not speak on his own authority: the Spirit's dependence on the Son is the same as the Son's dependence on the Father — perfect, voluntary, non-diminishing. He will glorify me: the Spirit's entire ministry is Christ-centered, Christ-glorifying, Christ-revealing. Any spiritual movement that shifts the center from Christ to the Spirit's own activity has lost the Spirit's own stated purpose.

verseByVerse.quote: "All that the Father has is mine; therefore I said that he will take what is mine and declare it to you. A little while, and you will see me no longer; and again a little while, and you will see me."
verseByVerse.commentary: All that the Father has is mine: the comprehensive claim of the Son to the Father's resources — not a grab for divine property but the natural statement of their shared nature. The Spirit mediates the Son's fullness to the church: everything in the divine treasury flows from Father to Son to Spirit to the church. A little while, and you will see me no longer; again a little while, and you will see me: the riddle of absence and return — the cross will hide him, the resurrection will reveal him. The little while has the elasticity of divine time: real anguish, real return, the shape of all Christian experience.

verseByVerse.quote: So some of his disciples said to one another, "What is this that he says to us, 'A little while, and you will not see me, and again a little while, and you will see me'; and, 'because I am going to the Father'?" So they were saying, "What does he mean by 'a little while'? We do not know what he is talking about."
verseByVerse.commentary: The disciples' confusion is honest and endearing: they are trying to understand, talking among themselves, genuinely puzzled. The riddle of absence and return — the cross, the death, the resurrection — is not yet intelligible because the event that will make it intelligible has not yet occurred. This is the pre-Pentecost condition of even the most devoted disciples: partial understanding, genuine confusion, sincere seeking. Jesus does not rebuke the confusion; he addresses it with the image of childbirth that will give them a framework when the events unfold.

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus knew that they wanted to ask him, so he said to them, "Is this what you are asking yourselves, what I meant by saying, 'A little while and you will not see me, and again a little while and you will see me'? Truly, truly, I say to you, you will weep and lament, but the world will rejoice. You will be sorrowful, but your sorrow will turn into joy."
verseByVerse.commentary: Jesus knew that they wanted to ask: the pastoral omniscience that meets the disciples where they are before they can articulate their need. Their coming grief — weeping and lamenting at the crucifixion while the world celebrates — is named and validated. But your sorrow will turn into joy: not be replaced by joy (as if the sorrow never happened) but transform into joy, as the same event that produced grief (the cross) is understood as the ground of joy (the resurrection, the atonement, the gift of the Spirit). The sorrow and the joy share the same object: the death and resurrection of the Son of God.

verseByVerse.quote: "When a woman is giving birth, she has sorrow because her hour has come, but when she has delivered the baby, she no longer remembers the anguish, for joy that a human being has been born into the world. So also you have sorrow now, but I will see you again, and your hearts will rejoice, and no one will take your joy from you."
verseByVerse.commentary: The childbirth image is perfect: the same event (labor) is anguish before and joy after; the anguish does not negate the joy but is the pathway to it. So also you have sorrow now: the cross will be anguish. But I will see you again: the resurrection appearance, the Pentecost presence, the final parousia — all are the 'seeing again' that produces the joy. No one will take your joy from you: resurrection joy is indestructible because its basis (the risen Christ) is indestructible. Circumstantial joy can be taken; the joy rooted in the resurrection and the Spirit's witness cannot be extinguished by any power in heaven or earth.

verseByVerse.quote: "In that day you will ask nothing of me. Truly, truly, I say to you, whatever you ask of the Father in my name, he will give it to you. Until now you have asked nothing in my name. Ask, and you will receive, that your joy may be full."
verseByVerse.commentary: In that day — the post-resurrection, post-Pentecost era — prayer operates in a new mode: in Jesus' name, directed to the Father, mediated by the Spirit. Until now you have asked nothing in my name: the disciples have prayed, but not with the full understanding of what it means to pray in and through the completed work of the Son. Ask, and you will receive, that your joy may be full: prayer is presented not as duty but as the pathway to the full joy Jesus has been promising throughout this discourse. The invitation is open, the name is given, the Father listens — the disciples need only to ask with the confidence that the name they carry is the guarantee of their hearing.

verseByVerse.quote: "I have said these things to you in figures of speech. The hour is coming when I will no longer speak to you in figures of speech but will tell you plainly about the Father. In that day you will ask in my name, and I do not say to you that I will ask the Father on your behalf;"
verseByVerse.commentary: In figures of speech: much of the farewell discourse has used the indirect language of vine, shepherd, bread, water — figures that point beyond themselves. The hour is coming — after the resurrection, through the Spirit — when the meaning will be plain. I do not say that I will ask on your behalf: not that Jesus no longer intercedes (he always lives to intercede, Heb. 7:25) but that the disciples' access to the Father is direct, through the Son's name, not requiring an intermediary to carry their requests. The Son's mediation is not distance but access; the name of Jesus opens the door, not stands between the petitioner and the Father.

verseByVerse.quote: "for the Father himself loves you, because you have loved me and have believed that I came from God. I came from the Father and have come into the world, and now I am leaving the world and going to the Father."
verseByVerse.commentary: The Father himself loves you: the disciples' access to the Father is not reluctantly granted through a reluctant Son interceding with a reluctant Father. The Father himself loves those who love the Son. The chain of love runs from the Father to the Son to the disciples, and the disciples' love for the Son creates the occasion for the Father's direct love. I came from the Father and have come into the world, and now I am leaving: the entire arc of the incarnation in one sentence — origin, arrival, departure. The movement is complete: from eternity into time and back into eternity, having accomplished the Father's redemptive purpose.

verseByVerse.quote: His disciples said, "Ah, now you are speaking plainly and not using figurative speech! Now we know that you know all things and do not need anyone to question you; this is why we believe that you came from God."
verseByVerse.commentary: Now you are speaking plainly: the disciples experience a moment of clarity and express the faith that has been building throughout the discourse. Now we know that you know all things: omniscience as the ground of confidence in Jesus' authority. We believe that you came from God: the disciples' confession is genuine, but Jesus will immediately test it with the prediction of their scattering (v. 32). The clarity they experience is real but not yet tested; the faith they express is authentic but not yet refined by the fire of the passion. The distance between expressed faith and proved faith is always the cross.

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus answered them, "Do you now believe? Behold, the hour is coming, indeed it has come, when you will be scattered, each to his own home, and will leave me alone. Yet I am not alone, for the Father is with me."
verseByVerse.commentary: Do you now believe? — the question probes the foundation of their confidence. The hour is coming — indeed it has come: the disciples' scattering is imminent, happening even as they speak. Each to his own home: the specificity of the prediction is its own kind of mercy — Jesus is not surprised by their failure; he has accounted for it in advance. Yet I am not alone: the Father's presence in the darkest moment is Jesus' own source of peace. The one who will face the cross abandoned by his disciples is not abandoned by his Father — yet — though the desolation of Golgotha will briefly shadow even that. The Father's presence is the source of the peace Jesus offers.

verseByVerse.quote: "I have said these things to you, that in me you may have peace. In the world you will have tribulation. But take heart; I have overcome the world."
verseByVerse.commentary: In the world you will have tribulation: not might, not possibly, but will. This is the sober realism of the farewell discourse — no promise of exemption from suffering, persecution, scattering, grief. But take heart; I have overcome the world: the word is already accomplished — the victory is already won, even though the disciples are about to experience it as defeat. The cross is the moment when the world thinks it has conquered and the resurrection is the moment when the conquest is revealed. The disciples face tribulation inside a victory that has already been secured. This is the peace Jesus offers: not absence of trouble but presence of the overcomer.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–26 — Jesus Prays for Himself, the Disciples, and All Believers
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Chapter 17 is the longest recorded prayer of Jesus, spoken before the arrest as both farewell and intercession. He prays for his own glorification (vv. 1-5), for the eleven who remain (vv. 6-19), and for all who will believe through their testimony (vv. 20-26). It is the theological summit of the fourth gospel, containing the most sustained exposition of the Son's relationship with the Father and his prayer for the church's unity.
verseByVerse.theology: The prayer is called the High-Priestly Prayer because it parallels the High Priest's prayer on the Day of Atonement — the one moment in the year when the high priest entered the Most Holy Place to intercede for the people. Jesus is simultaneously the priest and the sacrifice; he intercedes for his people while preparing himself for the offering that will accomplish what he prays for. His prayer for their sanctification (v. 17), protection (v. 11), joy (v. 13), and unity (v. 21-23) is the charter of the church's life.
verseByVerse.examples: That they may be one, as we are one (v. 22): the unity Jesus prays for is patterned on and derived from the inner-Trinitarian unity of Father and Son. This is not organizational uniformity or ecclesiastical merger but the living unity of love, shared purpose, and mutual indwelling. The church's unity is the Father's means of witnessing to the world (v. 21, 23): the divided church contradicts its own evangelistic witness. The prayer for unity is also the prayer for effective mission — they are inseparable in Jesus' own intercession.

verseByVerse.quote: When Jesus had spoken these words, he lifted up his eyes to heaven, and said, "Father, the hour has come; glorify your Son that the Son may glorify you, since you have given him authority over all flesh, to give eternal life to all whom you have given him."
verseByVerse.commentary: Father, the hour has come: the moment that the entire gospel has been building toward is now named in prayer. Glorify your Son: not a self-aggrandizing request but a Trinitarian one — the Son's glorification through the cross and resurrection will glorify the Father, because the Father's redeeming love will be fully displayed. Authority over all flesh: the universal scope of the Son's redemptive mission, given by the Father. To give eternal life to all whom you have given him: election and the gift of eternal life are correlated — the Father has given specific persons to the Son, and the Son gives them eternal life. None of those given will fail to receive it.

verseByVerse.quote: "And this is eternal life, that they know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent. I glorified you on earth, having accomplished the work that you gave me to do."
verseByVerse.commentary: This is eternal life, that they know you: the most important definition of eternal life in the New Testament. Eternal life is not primarily duration but relationship — knowing the only true God and Jesus Christ whom he sent. The Greek ginosko carries relational depth: the knowing of intimate, personal, covenantal relationship, not merely intellectual acquaintance with facts about God. I have accomplished the work: spoken from the threshold of the cross as if it is already done. The prayer treats the crucifixion as accomplished — the eternal Son, who operates in eternal time, speaks the cross as past even as he walks toward Gethsemane.

verseByVerse.quote: "And now, Father, glorify me in your own presence with the glory that I had with you before the world existed. I have manifested your name to the people whom you gave me out of the world. Yours they were, and you gave them to me, and they have kept your word."
verseByVerse.commentary: The glory that I had with you before the world existed: the pre-incarnate glory of the eternal Son, temporarily veiled in the humility of the incarnation, now to be fully restored in the resurrection and ascension. I have manifested your name: the entire ministry of Jesus — teaching, signs, foot-washing, and the cross — is the disclosure of the Father's name, his character, his love. Yours they were, and you gave them to me: the disciples belonged to the Father before they were given to the Son. Election is the Father's prior claim on the people the Son will redeem. They are not first the Son's and then the Father's; they are first the Father's and then, through gift, the Son's.

verseByVerse.quote: "Now they know that everything that you have given me is from you. For I have given them the words that you gave me, and they have received them and have come to know in truth that I came from you; and they have believed that you sent me."
verseByVerse.commentary: They have received the words and come to know that I came from you: the progression of the disciples' understanding — receiving the words, coming to know the divine origin, believing in the sending. This is the apostolic faith that will ground the New Testament: not a speculative philosophy but the reception of words given by the Father through the Son, producing the saving knowledge that Jesus is the sent one. They have believed that you sent me: this is the core of saving faith — that Jesus is the Father's envoy, carrying the Father's redemptive word and accomplishing the Father's saving purpose.

verseByVerse.quote: "I am praying for them. I am not praying for the world but for those whom you have given me, for they are yours. All mine are yours, and yours are mine, and I am glorified in them."
verseByVerse.commentary: I am not praying for the world: a clarification of the specific scope of this part of the prayer, not a statement of indifference to the world (v. 21, 23 will pray for the believing world). This prayer is the intercessory intercession of the High Priest for his people — specific, named, elect. All mine are yours, and yours are mine: the perfect mutual ownership of Father and Son extends to encompass the disciples. They belong simultaneously to the Father (given to the Son) and to the Son (who gives them eternal life). I am glorified in them: the disciples' existence is the Son's ongoing glory — the exhibition of what grace produces in those who receive it.

verseByVerse.quote: "And I am no longer in the world, but they are in the world, and I am coming to you. Holy Father, keep them in your name, which you have given me, that they may be one, even as we are one. While I was with them, I kept them in your name, which you have given me. I have guarded them, and not one of them has been lost except the son of destruction, that the Scripture might be fulfilled."
verseByVerse.commentary: Keep them in your name: the prayer for the disciples' preservation after Jesus' departure. Their security in the world does not rest on their own spiritual strength but on the Father's keeping power. That they may be one, even as we are one: the Trinitarian unity as the pattern and source of ecclesial unity — not organizational but relational, not uniformity but the unity of shared love and purpose. Not one of them has been lost except the son of destruction: the eleven's preservation is contrasted with Judas' defection, which is not a failure of the keeping power but the fulfillment of the Scripture — divine sovereignty encompassing even apostasy.

verseByVerse.quote: "But now I am coming to you, and these things I speak in the world, that they may have my joy fulfilled in themselves. I have given them your word, and the world has hated them because they are not of the world, just as I am not of the world."
verseByVerse.commentary: That they may have my joy fulfilled in themselves: the joy Jesus has in the Father's presence and in the accomplishment of the Father's will — this is what he prays will fill the disciples. Joy is not incidental to Christian life but its intended condition. I have given them your word: the word that has separated them from the world is the same word that sustains them through the world's hatred. The world hates because the disciples are not of the world — the election that brings them out of the world's system makes them targets of its hostility. The cross of the disciples is the natural consequence of the election that saved them.

verseByVerse.quote: "I do not ask that you take them out of the world, but that you keep them from the evil one. They are not of the world, just as I am not of the world."
verseByVerse.commentary: Not take them out of the world: the Christian life is not withdrawal from culture but engaged presence within it under divine protection. The prayer is for preservation in the world, not extraction from it. Keep them from the evil one: the specific threat named — not suffering or persecution but the evil one whose strategy is to snatch them from the Father's hand (10:28-29). The prayer for protection is precisely the Father's answer to the enemy's strategy. They are not of the world: the ontological status — belonging to the new creation, to the kingdom of God, to the Father — remains even while they inhabit the old world. Citizens of heaven on embassy in the world.

verseByVerse.quote: "Sanctify them in the truth; your word is truth. As you sent me into the world, so I have sent them into the world."
verseByVerse.commentary: Sanctify them in the truth: the word hagiazō (sanctify) means to set apart for holy purpose — the same word applied to Jesus' own consecration (v. 19). The disciples are to be made holy by the truth — the word of God that is the means of ongoing sanctification. Your word is truth: the Scriptures as the instrument of the Spirit's sanctifying work. As you sent me into the world, so I have sent them: the mission of the disciples is patterned on and derived from the mission of the Son. The Father sent the Son; the Son sends the disciples. The same commission, the same authority, the same purpose — world-mission in the Father's name.

verseByVerse.quote: "And for their sake I consecrate myself, that they also may be sanctified in truth. I do not ask for these only, but also for those who will believe in me through their word,"
verseByVerse.commentary: I consecrate myself: the language of priestly sacrifice — Jesus sets himself apart as the holy offering that will accomplish the sanctification he prays for the disciples. His death is not incidental but the means of their holiness. Those who will believe through their word: the prayer expands beyond the eleven to encompass every believer throughout history, including those reading this prayer in every generation. The High-Priestly Prayer is an intercession that reaches forward in time, encompassing the entire church that the apostolic word will gather. Every Christian stands within the scope of this prayer.

verseByVerse.quote: "that they may all be one, just as you, Father, are in me, and I in you, that they also may be in us, so that the world may believe that you have sent me. The glory that you have given me I have given to them, that they may be one even as we are one,"
verseByVerse.commentary: That they may all be one: the great prayer for ecclesial unity, patterned explicitly on Trinitarian unity. The church's unity is not achieved by human effort but given by participation in the Trinitarian life — they may be in us. The purpose is missional: so that the world may believe that you have sent me. The divided church is the church whose witness is compromised; the united church is the church whose common life is itself an argument for the gospel. The glory given to the disciples — the shared life of the Son — is the source of the unity that becomes the world's witness.

verseByVerse.quote: "I in them and you in me, that they may become perfectly one, so that the world may know that you sent me and loved them even as you loved me. Father, I desire that they also, whom you have given me, may be with me where I am, to see my glory that you have given me because you loved me before the foundation of the world."
verseByVerse.commentary: You loved them even as you loved me: the astonishing statement that the Father's love for the disciples is of the same kind as the Father's love for the Son.
